title: Thermodynamic Speed Limits In Isolated Quantum Systems
authors: Rikuya Kobashi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive thermodynamic speed limits for isolated quantum systems undergoing finite-time unitary driving. The key ingredient is a set of generalized second-law inequalities: for the Gibbs entropy and for several thermodynamically motivated observational entropies, the entropy production is bounded from below by a function of the Vu--Saito quantum Wasserstein distance between the initial and final coarse-grained states. These inequalities yield lower bounds on the operation time in terms of the average entropy-production rate. We apply the framework to system--bath coarse-graining, local-energy coarse-graining, and diagonal entropy, and illustrate the resulting bounds with numerical and analytically solvable examples. Our results provide a thermodynamic characterization of finite-time state transformations in isolated quantum systems and clarify how coarse-grained entropy production constrains macroscopic reachability.
tldr: The paper derives thermodynamic speed limits for isolated quantum systems under finite-time unitary driving using generalized second-law inequalities and quantum Wasserstein distances.
motivation: There is a need to characterize fundamental limits on finite-time state transformations in isolated quantum systems, connecting entropy production to operation time.
method: The authors prove generalized second-law inequalities for Gibbs entropy and thermodynamically motivated observational entropies, bounding entropy production below by a function of the Vu-Saito quantum Wasserstein distance between initial and final coarse-grained states.
result: These inequalities yield lower bounds on operation time in terms of the average entropy-production rate, applied to system-bath coarse-graining, local-energy coarse-graining, and diagonal entropy, with numerical and analytically solvable examples.
conclusion: The framework provides a thermodynamic characterization of finite-time state transformations in isolated quantum systems and clarifies how coarse-grained entropy production constrains macroscopic reachability.

title: Certifying Hidden Dissipation From Observed Current Fluctuations
authors: Ahmed Roman
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A single-molecule experiment on a driven enzyme or motor resolves only a few of the transitions the machine makes, yet one would like to know how much free energy it dissipates in total, including on the steps that stay hidden. The mean and the fluctuations of the currents on the watched transitions are shown to certify this hidden dissipation, with no knowledge of the transition rates and no access to the hidden transitions: when the watched transitions span the cycles of the network, the observed-current covariance recovers the full density-contracted quadratic current geometry, including the contribution of transitions that are never seen. The mechanism is that fluctuations are set by the dynamical activity, or traffic, the symmetric partner of the current. Contracting the large-deviation cost of empirical currents over density fluctuations identifies the observed-current covariance with a traffic-weighted metric, and turns partial observation into a minimum-energy completion problem over the unseen cycles, whose solution is the certified hidden cost. Existing current-fluctuation uncertainty relations bound dissipation from chosen currents but do not say when partial observation fixes the hidden contribution; the cycle-observability condition derived here does. The statements concern long-time means and fluctuations; finite-time estimates require separate error control.
tldr: The paper shows that the mean and fluctuations of observed currents can certify hidden dissipation in a partially observed stochastic network without knowing transition rates or hidden transitions.
motivation: In single-molecule experiments on driven enzymes or motors, only some transitions are resolved, yet one wants the total free-energy dissipation including the hidden steps.
method: Using large-deviation theory for empirical currents, the work contracts the dynamical-activity cost over density fluctuations to identify the observed-current covariance with a traffic-weighted metric and solves a minimum-energy completion over unseen cycles.
result: When observed transitions span the network cycles, the observed-current covariance recovers the full density-contracted current geometry and yields a certified hidden dissipation cost; a cycle-observability condition specifies when partial observation fixes the hidden contribution.
conclusion: The result extends current-fluctuation uncertainty relations by showing when hidden dissipation can be certified from partial observations, for long-time means and fluctuations, while finite-time estimates require separate error control.

title: Violating A Bell Inequality: What To Do When You Lose Your Quantum System
authors: Xinyu Xu, Yuqing Li, Mingze Xu, Dawei Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The detection loophole is a well-known loophole in Bell nonlocality motivated by the inefficiency of detectors used in Bell experiments. However, this inefficiency is actually a ubiquitous feature of any photonic platform for quantum networks since photons are readily absorbed by the surrounding environment. When the quantum system, usually a photon, is lost, what should the parties output? The most natural choice is to fall back to a deterministic strategy where each party produces an output via a function of her local input. In this paper, we study how to choose such a fallback strategy for general Bell inequalities with respect to different efficiencies [MATH] to maximize the possible violation. We mathematically prove that for the CHSH inequality, there exists a fallback strategy that is optimal for all [MATH]. However, in general, we find that the optimal fallback strategy can vary with [MATH], sometimes in surprising ways. For example, we find an example of a Bell inequality where the optimal fallback strategy near the threshold efficiency is not an optimal deterministic strategy in the lossless setting. Our results can reduce the efficiency requirements for closing the detection loophole and thus are useful for applications of Bell inequality violation, such as quantum telepathy or device-independent quantum key distribution.
tldr: This paper studies optimal deterministic fallback strategies for parties when their quantum system is lost in Bell tests, reducing detection-efficiency requirements for closing the detection loophole.
motivation: Photon loss is ubiquitous in photonic quantum networks and Bell experiments, and the detection loophole must be closed for device-independent applications such as DI-QKD.
method: The authors formulate the problem of choosing a fallback deterministic strategy to maximize Bell violation for general Bell inequalities as a function of detection efficiency, and mathematically analyze optimal strategies.
result: For the CHSH inequality, a single fallback strategy is optimal for all efficiencies; for general Bell inequalities, the optimal fallback can vary with efficiency and may not be an optimal deterministic strategy in the lossless setting.
conclusion: These results reduce the efficiency requirements for closing the detection loophole and are useful for applications of Bell inequality violation, including quantum telepathy and device-independent quantum key distribution.

title: Log-depth Entanglement Transition In Hypercube Gaussian Boson Sampling
authors: Alexey V. Gorshkov Laura Shou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an entanglement transition at logarithmic depth in random hypercube linear optical networks. Starting from an initial Gaussian state with all modes squeezed, we prove that random hypercube linear optical networks on [MATH] modes generate ensemble-averaged subsystem entanglement within a constant factor of its maximum in all subsystems at circuit depth [MATH]. Below depth [MATH], there is an extensive subsystem with no entanglement. The entanglement generation in logarithmic depth can be compared to recent progress towards [MATH] depth average-case sampling hardness for Gaussian boson sampling in a hypercube network.
tldr: The paper proves a logarithmic-depth entanglement transition in random hypercube linear optical networks used for Gaussian boson sampling.
motivation: Understanding how entanglement builds up in Gaussian boson sampling is important for connecting entanglement generation to the average-case sampling hardness of these photonic devices.
method: The authors analyze random hypercube linear optical networks acting on an initial Gaussian state with all modes squeezed and prove depth thresholds for ensemble-averaged subsystem entanglement.
result: At depth O(log M), every subsystem's entanglement is within a constant factor of its maximum; below this depth, an extensive subsystem remains completely unentangled.
conclusion: This establishes a sharp log-depth entanglement transition in hypercube Gaussian boson sampling networks, linking entanglement growth to recent progress on sampling hardness.

title: Dephasing-driven Suppression Of Superradiance And Metastable Dynamics In The Anisotropic Open Rabi Model
authors: Jivyanshu Priya, Pragna Das, Auditya Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite-component light-matter systems realize dissipative phase transitions in a single controllable atom-cavity setup, but how atomic dephasing - ubiquitous in real cavity- and circuit-QED devices - affects this criticality remains unknown. We study the anisotropic open Rabi model under cavity decay, spontaneous emission, and atomic dephasing together. We show that when spontaneous emission stabilizes a long-lived metastable superradiant phase, atomic dephasing actively competes with it - eroding its coherence and shortening the lifetime. This direct competition reveals that a dissipation channel's microscopic character, not its strength, controls its nonequilibrium criticality - a distinction directly tunable via independent spontaneous-emission and dephasing rates in circuit-QED and trapped-ion platforms.
tldr: Atomic dephasing suppresses and shortens the metastable superradiant phase in the anisotropic open Rabi model, showing that a dissipation channel's microscopic character controls nonequilibrium criticality.
motivation: Atomic dephasing is ubiquitous in real cavity- and circuit-QED devices, but its effect on dissipative phase transitions in finite-component light-matter systems was previously unknown.
method: The authors analyze the anisotropic open Rabi model including cavity decay, spontaneous emission, and atomic dephasing through open-system master-equation techniques.
result: Spontaneous emission can stabilize a long-lived metastable superradiant phase, while atomic dephasing competes with it, eroding coherence and shortening the phase lifetime.
conclusion: The competition reveals that the microscopic character of a dissipation channel, not just its strength, determines nonequilibrium criticality, and this distinction is tunable via independent rates in circuit-QED and trapped-ion platforms.

title: Travelling Dark State Polariton As A Viable Quantum Memory In A Solid-State Medium
authors: Shrabana Chakrabarti Avirup Chakraborty
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theorize a quantum memory based on the dark-state polariton field, formed by the superposition of atomic and photonic states of a travelling probe laser pulse under the application of standing wave modes of a dominant control laser pulse using a lambda-level scheme Electromagnetically Induced Transparency in a solid medium. We show how an enhancement in the storage time for the pulse is achieved by eliminating pulse broadening due to diffusion. tldr: The paper proposes a dark-state polariton based quantum memory in a solid-state EIT medium that enhances storage time by eliminating diffusion-induced pulse broadening.
motivation: Long-lived quantum memories are essential for quantum networks and repeaters, motivating solid-state implementations with extended storage times.
method: The authors theoretically analyze a lambda-level EIT scheme with a travelling probe pulse and standing-wave control field, deriving conditions to suppress diffusion broadening, and propose an experiment in cryogenically cooled hyperfine levels.
result: They show that the dark-state polariton storage time can be enhanced, and outline experimental parameters for probe pulse storage in a solid-state medium.
conclusion: The scheme is presented as a viable quantum memory for networking applications, with potential uses in quantum information processing.

title: Extended Wigner's Friend Scenarios With Agent-like Observers On Quantum Computers
authors: Eric G. Cavalcanti Joshua Laux
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Wigner's friend thought experiment raises the question of whether quantum theory can be applied consistently to systems that include observers. Extended Wigner's Friend Scenarios develop this question by considering several observers who may assign different descriptions to the same experiment. In the Local Friendliness (LF) framework, these scenarios lead to experimentally testable inequalities derived from assumptions such as Absoluteness of Observed Events and Local Agency. Motivated by the "Thoughtful" version of the Local Friendliness no-go theorem, which points towards future LF tests with human-level artificial agents implemented on quantum computers, this work implements the "friend" with explicit agent-like functionality within a reversible quantum circuit. Drawing from the literature on Artificial Intelligence, we construct rudimentary agent-like systems and embed them into a one-friend Extended Wigner's Friend Scenario. These agents store measurement outcomes, condition later operations on stored information, and, in the most structured case, use Born-rule probabilities to bet on the outcomes of their own future observations based on past observations. The circuits are simulated ideally and with an IBM-device noise model and executed on ibm_marrakesh. Ideal simulations reproduce the maximal quantum violation of a Local Friendliness inequality up to finite-shot fluctuations, while hardware runs show positive LF violations for all implemented agents. These results provide a first step towards more structured agent-like friend models in LF experiments on quantum computers.
tldr: Implements agent-like 'friend' observers in a one-friend Extended Wigner's Friend Scenario on quantum circuits, testing Local Friendliness inequalities on IBM hardware.
motivation: Motivated by the 'Thoughtful' Local Friendliness no-go theorem and the prospect of future LF tests with human-level artificial agents, this work bridges AI and quantum foundations by embedding agent-like functionality into quantum circuits.
method: Rudimentary agent-like systems that store measurement outcomes, condition later operations, and use Born-rule probabilities are constructed and embedded into reversible quantum circuits, then simulated ideally and with an IBM device noise model and executed on ibm_marrakesh.
result: Ideal simulations reproduce the maximal quantum violation of a Local Friendliness inequality up to finite-shot fluctuations, while hardware runs show positive LF violations for all implemented agents.
conclusion: This provides a first step towards more structured agent-like friend models in Local Friendliness experiments on quantum computers.

title: Sparse-Blossom Decoding In $o(1)$ Time
authors: Hayata Yamasaki Ryo Mikami
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matching-based decoding is widely used in quantum error correction, and accelerating it is key to enabling fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding provides rigorous guarantees for error suppression, while sparse blossom enables its practical implementation at modest problem sizes. However, the runtime of existing sparse-blossom implementations unavoidably increases with problem size, motivating a rigorous parallelization framework that guarantees correctness and a runtime shorter than the syndrome-extraction timescale. Here, we present such a framework and prove that the resulting parallel sparse-blossom algorithm produces the same correction as the original, non-parallel sparse blossom. For the rotated surface code with code distance [MATH] and physical error rates below a finite threshold, we prove that the average parallel runtime of decoding for [MATH] rounds of syndrome extraction is upper bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of [MATH]. For a [MATH]-round decoding window, this implies that the average parallel runtime per round is [MATH]. We also perform numerical simulation to identify conditions under which the parallel runtime per round decreases with increasing code distance. These results suggest that increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding.
tldr: A parallel sparse-blossom decoding framework for surface codes with proven correctness and quasi-polylogarithmic average runtime.
motivation: Matching-based decoding such as minimum-weight perfect matching is essential for quantum error correction, but existing sparse-blossom implementations scale poorly with problem size, limiting fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation.
method: The authors design a parallel sparse-blossom algorithm and prove it produces the same correction as the sequential sparse blossom, then bound its average parallel runtime for the rotated surface code below threshold.
result: For code distance d and physical error rates below a finite threshold, the average parallel runtime for d rounds of syndrome extraction is quasi-polylogarithmic in d, implying o(1) runtime per round in a decoding window; simulations identify conditions where per-round runtime decreases with increasing code distance.
conclusion: Increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding in fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Dynamical Qubit Cooling Via Quasi-particle Transport
authors: Jasmin Bedow Kyle Monkman
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooling a quantum state presents a challenge as the external control in active protocols can induce detrimental heating in the system. Passive cooling processes offer a valuable alternative: Here, we present a simple quench protocol to cool a set of qubits with access to an ancillary spin chain. We show that excitations can be transported out of the qubits as quasi-particles, taking the form of magnons in a ferromagnetic ancilla and triplons in a dimerized antiferromagnetic ancilla. This quasi-particle transport mechanism enables cooling towards both individual and highly entangled two-qubit target states. We demonstrate that this cooling mechanism remains robust starting from thermal states and with finite quench ramp times.
tldr: A quench protocol cools qubits by transporting excitations as quasiparticles into an ancillary spin chain.
motivation: Active cooling schemes can induce detrimental heating, so passive cooling alternatives are needed for quantum state preparation.
method: The authors use a ferromagnetic ancilla supporting magnons or a dimerized antiferromagnetic ancilla supporting triplons to transport excitations away from the qubits via a quench protocol.
result: The mechanism cools toward individual and highly entangled two-qubit target states and remains robust when starting from thermal states and with finite quench ramp times.
conclusion: Quasiparticle transport in spin chains provides a simple and robust passive route for dynamical qubit cooling, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and state engineering.

title: Hardware Fingerprinting Ftqc Via Quantum Decoder Timing
authors: Friedrich Doku, Jakub Szefer, Kaitlin N. Smith
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the quantum computing field transitions toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC), intensive efforts are focused on scaling architectures and realizing active error correction. However, this shift introduces security surfaces that remain largely unexplored. Fault-tolerant quantum computers pair a quantum processor with a classical decoder that sits on the critical path of every syndrome-extraction round. For the first time, this work demonstrates that the wall-clock time each decoder takes to process a syndrome measurement and decoding round constitutes a novel, exploitable hardware side channel on physical quantum hardware. Using per-shot decoder timings from three IBM Heron processors collected over a 68-day window, the decode-time distribution alone allows a passive observer to (i) reconstruct the shot-by-shot detector-firing distribution and estimate the workload's logical error rate [MATH], (ii) infer the code distance in use, and (iii) fingerprint the specific physical device with up to 89% accuracy (a random guess is 33%), with a pooled two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test confirming the decode-time distributions are statistically distinct. In noisy simulation inspired by public data from Google's 105-qubit Willow processor, decoder timing further distinguishes 9 surface-code patches at different locations on the chip with 81% accuracy, showing the side channel persists on below-threshold fault-tolerant hardware from a different vendor and code family.
tldr: Decoder wall-clock timing in fault-tolerant quantum computers acts as a hardware side channel that can reconstruct detector firing distributions, infer code distance, and fingerprint specific quantum processors.
motivation: As quantum computing moves toward fault-tolerant operation, the classical decoder on the syndrome-extraction critical path introduces an unexplored security surface.
method: The authors analyze per-shot decoder timing data from three IBM Heron processors over 68 days, using statistical tests and noisy simulations of Google Willow surface-code patches to assess information leakage.
result: Decoder timing allows estimation of logical error rates, inference of code distance, device fingerprinting with up to 89% accuracy, and distinguishes nine chip locations with 81% accuracy.
conclusion: Decoder timing is a persistent and exploitable side channel on below-threshold fault-tolerant hardware, with implications for the security of future quantum computing systems.

title: Modeling Quantum Error Detection With Transition Matrices
authors: Rohan S. Kumar, Ben Foxman, Yongshan Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct an explicit transition matrix that exactly describes code-adapted basis-population dynamics of stabilizer codes under circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise. The matrix is expressed in a code-adapted basis that captures probability flow between logical-basis labels and syndrome sectors. For quantum error detection (QED), we incorporate post-selection by aggregating rejected outcomes into an absorbing state, so that a single transition matrix represents a full clock cycle of gates, syndrome extraction, and post-selection. Additionally, we characterize when protocol symmetries permit exact lumping to simpler, more interpretable models. The transition matrix framework enables direct application of classical stochastic-matrix techniques to analyze multi-cycle QED protocols. First, we identify a leading-order obstruction to a stationary logical-only accepted-map description, and quantify the accepted leakage injection from QED-check imperfections that causes it. Second, we express leading-order QED efficiency as a function of check frequency in terms of physically meaningful parameters, and prove that less frequent checks improve efficiency to leading order. We evaluate the framework on the [MATH] and [MATH] codes under depolarizing gate noise and readout errors: transition-matrix predictions agree with million-shot Stim Monte Carlo at the scale of the reported confidence intervals, and matrix-computed results illustrate the first-cycle transient and interval-dependent efficiency. More broadly, the transition-matrix formalism provides both an analytical foundation for QED analysis and an interpretable tool for understanding code behavior under realistic noise.
tldr: The paper introduces a transition-matrix framework for modeling code-adapted basis-population dynamics in quantum error detection with stabilizer codes under circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise and post-selection.
motivation: Quantum error detection protocols require understanding multi-cycle behavior, leakage, and efficiency under realistic noise, but existing analyses often lack an explicit stochastic-dynamics description.
method: The authors construct a transition matrix in a code-adapted basis that tracks probability flow between logical-basis labels and syndrome sectors, incorporate post-selection via an absorbing rejected state, characterize symmetry-induced lumping, and validate predictions against million-shot Stim Monte Carlo on two codes.
result: They identify a leading-order obstruction to a stationary logical-only accepted-map description, quantify accepted leakage from QED-check imperfections, and prove that less frequent checks improve leading-order QED efficiency; numerical results show first-cycle transients and interval-dependent efficiency.
conclusion: The transition-matrix formalism provides an analytical and interpretable tool for analyzing multi-cycle QED protocols and code behavior under realistic circuit-level noise.

title: Evidencing Macroscopic Quantum Coherence Using Confined Uniform Magnetic Field
authors: Dipankar Home, Harsh Talwar, Nilaj Saha, Sougato Bose, Arka Banerjee
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A previously unexplored scheme is devised for creating and certifying coherent quantum superposition of distinctly separated states of a spin-tagged massive object passing through a confined uniform magnetic field. This results in entangling the spatial and spin parts of a two-component Pauli wavefunction such that the entailed coherence can be conveniently certified by spin measurements alone. The implementability of this scheme is analysed using NV-centre nanodiamonds of masses [MATH] amu based on the current technological capabilities.
tldr: A new scheme uses a confined uniform magnetic field to create and certify coherent spatial superposition of a spin-tagged massive object via spin measurements alone, with feasibility analyzed for NV-centre nanodiamonds.
motivation: Certifying genuine quantum coherence and superposition in increasingly massive objects is central to testing the quantum-classical boundary and to developing macroscopic quantum technologies, but existing schemes require challenging position-sensitive measurements.
method: The authors devise a two-component Pauli wavefunction in which passage through a confined uniform magnetic field entangles the spatial and spin degrees of freedom, so that coherence in the spatial sector can be certified purely through spin measurements; they assess experimental implementability with NV-centre nanodiamonds.
result: The scheme yields an entangled spin-spatial state whose coherence witnesses are accessible via spin readout alone, and parameter estimates suggest feasibility for nanodiamond masses on the order of 10^6 amu given current technology.
conclusion: The proposal offers a practical, measurement-simplified route to evidencing macroscopic quantum coherence, complementing established NV-centre superposition experiments and motivating near-term tabletop tests.

title: Extremely Low-Cost Magic State Preparation Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
authors: Jianshuo Gao, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant preparation of non-Clifford resource states is a major contributor to the overhead of quantum computation, motivating protocols that achieve high output fidelity with minimal qubit and circuit costs. We introduce a low-cost magic-state preparation protocol in which the choice of stabilizer generators is co-designed with the flag gadgets, allowing the syndrome-extraction circuit itself to filter correlated faults across a non-Clifford layer. The protocol prepares a logical plus state in the 15-qubit quantum Reed-Muller code, applies a transversal T gate, and gauge-fixes the same register into the seven-qubit Steane code. By reorganizing equivalent Z-type stabilizer generators into jointly flagged measurement groups, the protocol eliminates all accepted logical-error contributions arising from one or two circuit faults under destructive error detection. Under a uniform circuit-level depolarizing noise model, the postselected infidelity is [MATH]. At [MATH], exact low-order enumeration combined with stratified sampling bounds the infidelity by [MATH] at 99.9% joint confidence, while retaining an acceptance probability of 86.9%. The complete circuit requires only 19 qubits and 82 CNOT gates. These results demonstrate that stabilizer-generator design can substantially reduce the cost of postselected magic-state preparation, although corrected operation and the fidelity of an unmeasured output block require separate analysis.

motivation: Fault-tolerant preparation of non-Clifford resource states dominates the overhead of quantum computation, so protocols achieving high output fidelity with minimal qubit and gate cost are highly desirable.
method: The protocol prepares a logical plus state in the 15-qubit quantum Reed-Muller code, applies a transversal T gate, and gauge-fixes into the seven-qubit Steane code; equivalent Z-type stabilizer generators are reorganized into jointly flagged measurement groups so the syndrome-extraction circuit itself filters correlated faults.
result: Under uniform circuit-level depolarizing noise, the postselected infidelity is tightly bounded via exact low-order enumeration plus stratified sampling at 99.9% joint confidence while retaining an 86.9% acceptance probability, using only 19 qubits and 82 CNOT gates, eliminating all accepted logical-error contributions from one or two circuit faults.
conclusion: Stabilizer-generator design can substantially reduce the cost of postselected magic-state preparation, though corrected operation and the fidelity of an unmeasured output block remain to be analyzed separately.

title: Staying Positive: Bounds For non-Gaussian Noise In Schwinger-Keldysh Effective Field Theory
authors: Daniel K. Brattan Andrea Amoretti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern effective field theories of dissipative hydrodynamics, built on the Schwinger-Keldysh (SK) formalism, include thermal noise that is not Gaussian. The resultant higher-order noise vertices are constrained by symmetries, but otherwise treated as free parameters. We show explicitly that symmetry constraints alone do not guarantee these vertices yield a genuine probability distribution. Requiring a probability interpretation yields sharp bounds between cumulants that are invisible to the symmetry analysis. The bounds are optimal: their boundaries are attained by explicit positive distributions, and constructive completions are provided for both negative- and positive-kurtosis noise data. This gives closed-form nonlinear response and an exact sampling algorithm, whose Monte Carlo implementation reproduces the exact cumulants and nonlinear fluctuation-dissipation relations. Confronted with microscopic results, the framework places a sharp lower bound on the time step required for a positive stochastic completion of a quartic model of the Brownian particle used in the literature, while holographically computed [MATH] noise vertices pass a nontrivial continuum fourth-order positivity test.
tldr: Symmetry constraints alone do not guarantee a positive probability distribution for non-Gaussian noise in Schwinger-Keldysh effective field theory; requiring a probability interpretation yields sharp, optimal bounds on cumulants and nonlinear fluctuation-dissipation relations.
motivation: Modern effective field theories of dissipative hydrodynamics include non-Gaussian thermal noise with higher-order vertices treated as free parameters, but it is unclear whether symmetries alone ensure a consistent probabilistic interpretation.
method: The authors analyze cumulant constraints imposed by positivity of the noise distribution, construct explicit positive distributions that attain the bounds, and provide closed-form nonlinear response, an exact sampling algorithm, and Monte Carlo tests against microscopic and holographic models.
result: They derive optimal bounds between cumulants, obtain a sharp lower bound on the time step for a positive stochastic completion of a quartic Brownian model, and show that holographically computed noise vertices pass a nontrivial continuum fourth-order positivity test.
conclusion: Requiring a genuine probability distribution imposes constraints beyond symmetry, with implications for consistent stochastic completions of dissipative hydrodynamic effective field theories and nonlinear fluctuation-dissipation relations.

title: Learning Sparse Quantum States
authors: Aniruddha Sen

tldr: This paper provides the first near-optimal algorithm for learning k-sparse pure quantum states, achieving optimal sample and time complexity up to polylog factors.
motivation: While classical distribution learning has tight sample and time bounds in terms of support size, no non-trivial bounds were previously known for tomography of sparse quantum states.
method: The author develops an algorithm for k-sparse pure states and extends it to k-sparse rank-r mixed states via the random purification channel technique.
result: The algorithm achieves fidelity at least 1-ε using O(k log n / ε^2) copies of an n-qubit state and comparable time; both bounds are optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.
conclusion: This resolves the sample complexity of sparse quantum state tomography, though achieving matching time complexity for k>1 remains an important open question.

title: Keyless Secrecy Against Bounded Adversaries
authors: Anne Broadbent, Upendra Kapshikar, Denis Rochette
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a keyless coding/cryptographic primitive that asks for two guarantees at once: the receiver is never fooled into accepting a message other than the one sent, and the adversary learns nothing about the message unless the receiver aborts. Neither the sender nor the receiver holds a secret key, and no computational hardness is assumed. The only restriction is on the adversary's online computation: the receiver aborts if nothing arrives by a fixed deadline, so the adversary must forward something before it, and her map in that window is computed by a circuit of size (or depth) at most [MATH]; before and after, she is unbounded. For every polynomial [MATH] we construct such an efficient quantum scheme, encoding [MATH]-bit messages into [MATH] qubits with circuits of size [MATH]. No classical scheme achieves this type of everlasting security, at any choice of parameters. Our techniques also resolve open questions about universal tamper detection against families restricted in cardinality rather than in circuit size. We settle a question of Broadbent, Kapshikar and Rochette on relaxed tamper detection. As a corollary, we obtain the first efficient non-malleable code secure against global quantum tampering, with no split-state restriction, whereas the current constructions in the literature require the codeword to be split into non-communicating shares.
tldr: The paper introduces a keyless quantum coding/cryptographic primitive that simultaneously guarantees tamper detection and secrecy against computationally bounded online adversaries, without keys or computational hardness assumptions.
motivation: Standard cryptographic secrecy relies on shared secret keys or computational hardness assumptions, and no classical scheme can achieve everlasting security in this setting. The authors seek a keyless primitive providing both tamper detection and message secrecy.
method: They construct efficient quantum schemes encoding m-bit messages into poly(m) qubits using polynomial-size circuits, exploiting the restriction that the adversary's online map within the deadline must be a small circuit (size or depth), while the adversary is otherwise unbounded. Techniques also yield universal tamper detection against cardinality-restricted adversary families.
result: For every polynomial they build such schemes with efficient encodings and circuits, prove no classical scheme achieves this everlasting security at any parameters, and as a corollary obtain the first efficient non-malleable code secure against global quantum tampering without a split-state restriction.
conclusion: The work resolves open questions on relaxed and universal tamper detection and advances quantum non-malleable codes, showing a genuine quantum advantage for keyless secrecy against bounded adversaries.

title: Security Implications Of Measurement Based Crosstalk On Superconducting Quantum Computers
authors: Kimmo Halunen Subarna Adhikari
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Crosstalk is one of the major issues for scalability of superconducting quantum processors. But it can also be used by threat actors to intentionally sabotage computations and steal information. This paper analyzes data leakage due to crosstalk during qubit measurement. Prior research yielded an accuracy of 96% in classifying measurement of one qubit in IBM quantum computers. When evaluated on superconducting hardware from VTT, we achieved an accuracy of 71.68% with similar framework. Our extended framework with additional labels yields an accuracy of 76.30% for classifying measurement of one qubit and 53.37% for measurement of two qubits using Support Vector Machine (SVM). Experimental results indicate that measurement operation on a qubit can affect the probability of measuring adjacent qubits. The impact on the target qubit is dependent on the number of neighboring qubits measured and also the measurement outcome.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that measurement-based crosstalk on superconducting quantum processors can leak information about neighboring qubits and be exploited by threat actors to sabotage computations or steal data.
motivation: Crosstalk is a known scalability bottleneck for superconducting processors, but its potential as a security vulnerability—enabling intentional sabotage or side-channel information leakage—has been underexplored.
method: The authors apply and extend a prior machine-learning/SVM classification framework to measurement data from VTT superconducting hardware, introducing additional labels to classify the measurement outcome of one and two qubits based on neighboring-qubit measurement effects.
result: Classification accuracy reached 71.68% (vs. 96% on IBM hardware) for single-qubit measurement and 76.30%/53.37% for one-/two-qubit measurement with the extended framework, showing that measuring one qubit shifts the measurement probabilities of adjacent qubits depending on the number and outcome of neighbors.
conclusion: Measurement crosstalk constitutes a genuine information-leakage and sabotage channel in superconducting quantum computers, motivating security-aware hardware design and calibration.

title: Design And Finite-Element Analysis Of A New Inclined Blade-Electrode Architecture For Trapped-Ion Quantum Information Processing
authors: Nahiyan Archa, Abhinand P, Ahammed Shabeeb, Nikhil Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The development of scalable quantum technologies requires ion-trap architectures that provide strong and stable confinement while minimizing motional heating caused by electric-field noise. Trapped-ion systems offer long coherence times and high-fidelity quantum control; however, anomalous motional heating from electrode surfaces can limit their performance. This study presents a finite-element analysis of a novel inclined ion-trap architecture, focusing on the effects of electrode geometry and blade separation on confinement strength, secular frequencies, motional heating, thermal response, and RF stability. Five trap inclinations were investigated using three-dimensional electrostatic simulations for blade separations of 5 to 35 um. The RF electric-field distribution was used to determine the effective pseudopotential, trap depth, secular frequencies, and normal modes. An empirical electric-field-noise model was then used to estimate the motional heating rate for frequency-noise exponents alpha = 3, 3.5, and 4. The results reveal a trade-off between confinement strength and ion-electrode distance. Blade separations of approximately 25 to 35 um provide a favorable design regime. At 25 um, the predicted heating rate is approximately 127 to 135 quanta per second for alpha = 3, but the RF stability margin is lower (qmax approximately 1.9). At 35 um, the stability is substantially improved (qmax approximately 0.52), while the heating rate increases to approximately 1570 to 1820 quanta per second. These results provide design guidelines for optimizing inclined ion traps for future trapped-ion quantum-information architectures.
tldr: A finite-element study of an inclined blade-electrode trapped-ion trap architecture, optimizing blade separation to balance confinement strength, RF stability, and motional heating.
motivation: Scalable trapped-ion quantum information processing requires stable ion confinement while minimizing anomalous motional heating from electrode-surface electric-field noise.
method: Three-dimensional electrostatic simulations were performed for five trap inclinations and blade separations from 5 to 35 um, extracting the pseudopotential, trap depth, secular frequencies, normal modes, and RF stability, with an empirical electric-field-noise model used to estimate heating rates for noise exponents alpha = 3, 3.5, and 4.
result: A trade-off is found between confinement and ion-electrode distance: 25-35 um blade separations are favorable; at 25 um the predicted heating is about 127-135 quanta/s but qmax is about 1.9, while at 35 um qmax improves to about 0.52 but heating rises to about 1570-1820 quanta/s.
conclusion: The results provide design guidelines for optimizing inclined ion traps for future trapped-ion quantum-information architectures, though they rely on simulation and empirical noise modeling rather than experimental demonstration.

title: A Simple Quantum Linear-System Solver Via Dissipation
authors: Zhong-Xia Shang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dissipation has been recently demonstrated as a powerful primitive for designing quantum algorithms. We apply this viewpoint directly to linear-system solving, [MATH]. We construct a simple purely dissipative Lindbladian whose unique fixed point encodes the linear-system solution. We prove dimension-independent trace-distance mixing in [MATH] time. We then show how to run this Lindbladian on digital quantum computers via collective block encoding and Lindbladian simulation, resulting in an [MATH] query complexity for both [MATH], the block encoding of [MATH], and [MATH], the [MATH] state preparation unitary.
tldr: The paper constructs a purely dissipative Lindbladian whose unique steady state encodes the solution of a linear system, and shows how to simulate it on a digital quantum computer.
motivation: Dissipation has recently emerged as a powerful algorithmic primitive, and the authors aim to apply this viewpoint directly to the problem of solving linear systems Ax=b.
method: They design an explicit Lindbladian with a unique fixed point equal to the linear-system solution, prove dimension-independent trace-distance mixing in logarithmic time, and implement the dynamics via collective block encoding and Lindbladian simulation on digital quantum computers.
result: They obtain polylogarithmic query complexity in terms of the block encoding of A and the state-preparation unitary, yielding a simple solver with favorable scaling.
conclusion: Dissipative dynamics provides a conceptually simple route to quantum linear-system solving, though the work is algorithmic in nature and does not draw on thermodynamic or information-theoretic bounds.

title: The Low-Individual-Degree Test Without The Diagonal-Lines Test Is Not Quantum-Sound
authors: Tianrun Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To prove the quantum soundness of the classical low-individual-degree test, the authors of defined three subtests, namely the axis-parallel lines test, the self-consistency test, and the diagonal-lines test. An interesting question is whether the diagonal-lines test can be removed. In this paper, we show that the diagonal-lines test cannot simply be removed without another compatibility mechanism. Consequently, replacing the "conditional linear functions" by "coordinate deletion functions" in the proof of MIP*=RE, as mentioned in , does not by itself preserve the required soundness. The authors of found an example that requires the diagonal-lines test when \((m, d, q) = (2, 2, 4)\); we give an example when \((m, d) = (2, 2)\) and \(q\) is any odd prime.
tldr: The diagonal-lines test cannot be removed from the low-individual-degree test without losing quantum soundness, as shown by a new counterexample.
motivation: To determine whether the diagonal-lines test is necessary for proving quantum soundness of the classical low-individual-degree test, which is relevant to the MIP*=RE proof.
method: Construct an explicit example for (m,d)=(2,2) and any odd prime q that violates quantum soundness when the diagonal-lines test is omitted, using coordinate deletion functions.
result: The diagonal-lines test is required for quantum soundness; replacing conditional linear functions with coordinate deletion functions does not preserve soundness.
conclusion: The diagonal-lines test provides a necessary compatibility mechanism, and its removal demands an alternative mechanism to maintain quantum soundness.

title: A Dichotomy For Boolean Complex Holant Problems With Conjugate-Closed Signature Sets
authors: Jincheng Guan, Shuai Shao, Zhuxiao Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.13132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Boolean Holant problems with complex-valued signature sets closed under conjugation. Such sets arise naturally in tensor-network expressions for classical strong simulation of quantum circuits. We prove a complexity dichotomy for such problems with an explicit tractability criterion. This extends the dichotomy for real-valued Holant problems, with the same four tractability conditions. Our proofs use Xia's projective binary group framework and quantum entanglement theory. The conjugate closure assumption precisely makes [MATH]-uniformity, directly applicable to the classification of Holant problems, by realizing reduced density matrices via Holant gadgets. We also use the classification of absolutely maximally entangled states to resolve a particular [MATH]-ary obstruction in our inductive proof of the \#P-hardness.
tldr: The paper proves a complexity dichotomy for Boolean Holant problems with conjugate-closed complex-valued signature sets, using quantum entanglement theory and the classification of absolutely maximally entangled states.
motivation: Holant problems generalize many counting problems and arise in tensor-network expressions for classical strong simulation of quantum circuits, but the complexity for complex-valued signature sets with conjugate closure was not fully understood.
method: The authors employ Xia's projective binary group framework to realize reduced density matrices via Holant gadgets, and they use the classification of absolutely maximally entangled states to resolve an obstruction in the inductive proof of #P-hardness.
result: They establish an explicit tractability criterion that extends the real-valued Holant dichotomy with the same four tractability conditions, and they prove #P-hardness otherwise.
conclusion: This work advances the complexity classification of Holant problems and illustrates a nontrivial application of quantum entanglement theory to computational complexity.

title: Tensor-network Monte Carlo Approach Based On Time-evolving Block Decimation
authors: Shimpei Goto, Hidemaro Suwa, Synge Todo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a tensor-network Monte Carlo (TNMC) approach for unitary evolution following the compression sequence of the time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) algorithm. In the TNMC approach, the obtained results contain evaluable statistical errors rather than truncation errors, unlike ordinary singular-value-decomposition-based methods such as the TEBD algorithm. Consequently, one can estimate unbiased expectation values within statistical errors even with a finite bond dimension. Since the sampling scheme is introduced in the simulations of unitary evolution, the proposed Monte Carlo scheme may suffer from a sign problem. We observe that the sign problem can be mitigated by increasing the bond dimension. We apply the proposed TNMC approach to the Hamiltonian and the Floquet dynamics. Numerical experiments show that the TNMC approach can estimate accurate expectation values of observables even when the TEBD method with the same bond dimension cannot. The proposed approach can be a new direction for improving the classical simulatability of unitary evolution.
tldr: A tensor-network Monte Carlo method based on TEBD compression is proposed for simulating unitary quantum evolution with statistical error estimates, mitigating the sign problem by increasing bond dimension.
motivation: Ordinary TEBD suffers from truncation errors that bias expectation values at finite bond dimension. The authors aim to obtain unbiased estimates with controllable statistical errors by introducing Monte Carlo sampling into the compression sequence.
method: The approach replaces deterministic truncation in TEBD with a stochastic sampling scheme over the tensor network compression, yielding evaluable statistical errors and allowing the sign problem to be mitigated by increasing the bond dimension.
result: Numerical experiments on Hamiltonian and Floquet dynamics show that the TNMC method estimates accurate observables even when TEBD with the same bond dimension fails, and the sign problem is observed to decrease with larger bond dimension.
conclusion: TNMC offers a new direction for improving classical simulatability of unitary evolution, trading truncation errors for statistical errors, at the cost of a potential sign problem that can be controlled.

title: A Survey On Quantum-Safe Cryptographic Mechanisms: Building Blocks And Applications
authors: Ricardo Parizotto, Preeti Yadav, Marcus Freire, Anderson Tomkelski, Maycon Peixoto, Emmanuel Zambrini Cruzeiro, Israat Haque
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The possible emergence of fault-tolerant quantum computers may enable widely used cryptographic algorithms to be broken. These algorithms for public key encryption and digital signatures could be exposed if an efficient algorithm is employed. This poses a threat to existing infrastructure, motivating the development of mechanisms that can withstand quantum-computer cybersecurity risks. However, the transition to new security mechanisms is still underway and faces many challenges, including identifying which applications are under threat and implementing agile, scalable migration processes. In this work, we survey the state of the art in quantum-safe cryptographic mechanisms, existing applications targeting migration, and open challenges. We examine the building blocks commonly used to integrate quantum-safe mechanisms into existing applications and categorize them by the security mechanisms they employ. Next, we systematically review existing migrations into quantum-safe schemes and categorize them by application domain, including Telecommunications, the Internet of Things, and Blockchains. Finally, we summarize the challenges that must be addressed to enable a successful migration to quantum-resistant mechanisms, as well as the motivations for pursuing this migration.
tldr: A survey of quantum-safe (post-quantum) cryptographic building blocks, migration efforts across application domains, and remaining open challenges.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computers threaten widely deployed public-key encryption and digital signatures, so existing infrastructure must migrate to quantum-resistant mechanisms, yet the transition is still incomplete and poorly mapped.
method: The authors survey state-of-the-art quantum-safe cryptographic mechanisms, categorize their building blocks by security mechanism, and systematically review existing migration case studies by application domain (telecommunications, IoT, blockchains).
result: The survey organizes quantum-safe primitives and migration approaches into a taxonomy, identifies which application domains have been addressed, and consolidates the technical and operational challenges hindering migration.
conclusion: Successful migration to quantum-resistant mechanisms requires agile, scalable processes and targeted effort across domains; the paper lays out motivations and open problems to guide this transition.

title: Quantum Neural Network Equipped With Backpropagation On A Qudit Processor
authors: Yibo Yuan, Zhuoyue Xu, Zhenyue Du, Xingyu Zhao, Xu Cheng, Yue Li, Waner Hou, Yuqi Zhou, Zhaokai Li, Yiheng Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs), one of the fundamental algorithms in quantum machine learning, have been widely used in classification and identification tasks. However, the capabilities of QNNs are constrained by their size, which is determined by the dimension of the Hilbert space of the underlying quantum processor. Multi-level quantum digits (qudits) offer access to a higher-dimensional Hilbert space compared to two-level qubits, enabling the construction of more expressive QNNs. In this work, we report an experimental demonstration of qudit-based QNN using a trapped [MATH] ion. We train the QNN using a hybrid quantum-classical implementation of backpropagation and achieve an experimental classification accuracy of [MATH] on a test image set. This demonstration highlights the potential of qudit-based processors to QNN architectures and provides a framework for implementing qudit-based QNNs across various quantum devices.
tldr: An experimental demonstration of a qudit-based quantum neural network trained with hybrid quantum-classical backpropagation on a trapped-ion processor, achieving high classification accuracy on a test image set.
motivation: QNN expressivity is limited by the Hilbert space dimension of the underlying processor, and qudits provide a larger space than qubits, potentially enabling more powerful QNNs.
method: The authors encode a QNN on a trapped-ion qudit processor and train it using a hybrid quantum-classical backpropagation algorithm, then evaluate it on an image classification task.
result: They report an experimental classification accuracy on a test image set, demonstrating that qudit-based QNNs can be realized on existing hardware.
conclusion: The work highlights qudit processors as a promising route to more expressive QNN architectures and offers a general framework for implementing them across platforms.

title: Error-Rate Reduction In Ldpc Decoding Via Bit-Aligned Temporal Reinforcement In Parallel Probabilistic-Bit Dynamics
authors: Takahiro Hanyu Naoya Onizawa
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Probabilistic bits (p-bits) provide a physical and algorithmic primitive for stochastic inference, but highly parallel updates can alter their collective dynamics. We study the decoding of random-regular (3, 6) low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes using Jacobi-type p-bit annealing with stochastic partial activation. An additive response-path rule stores each bit's saturated response and reuses it before stochastic readout. High-statistics simulations with independent parameter optimization for each method show pooled bit-error-rate reductions of 33.5%, 74.8%, and 81.8% relative to memoryless probabilistic simulated annealing (pSA) for representative codes of block lengths 96, 192, and 288, respectively. Static gain, normalized averaging, response shuffling, and same-bit binary-state feedback with only its coefficient tuned under the same nonmemory parameters do not reproduce the full saturated-response benefit. Trajectory analysis links the improvement to acquisition of the channel-consistent valid-codeword basin and enhanced post-acquisition stability; the acquisition advantage persists from random and channel-hard-decision starts under the tested conditions. Across all 30 independent code realizations, fixed additive parameter-and-readout packages achieve lower bit- and frame-error rates than separately optimized pSA-specific packages, with neither package retuned for individual codes. These results show that the computational effect of temporal state depends on the retained quantity and its reinjection into stochastic dynamics.
tldr: The paper introduces a bit-aligned temporal reinforcement technique for probabilistic-bit (p-bit) LDPC decoding, achieving significant bit-error-rate reductions compared to memoryless probabilistic simulated annealing.
motivation: Probabilistic bits offer a physical substrate for stochastic inference, but highly parallel updates can disrupt collective dynamics, motivating the need to retain temporal state to improve decoding performance.
method: The authors employ Jacobi-type p-bit annealing with stochastic partial activation and an additive response-path rule that stores and reuses each bit's saturated response before stochastic readout.
result: Simulations on (3,6) LDPC codes of lengths 96, 192, and 288 show bit-error-rate reductions of 33.5%, 74.8%, and 81.8% relative to memoryless pSA, with consistent gains across 30 code realizations.
conclusion: The computational benefit of temporal state depends on the retained quantity and its reinjection into stochastic dynamics, suggesting a path to improved p-bit-based decoding.

title: The Information Complexity Of Decision Trees
authors: Avantika Agarwal, Shalev Ben-David, Eric Blais
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We define and study a measure of information complexity for randomized decision trees. We prove three main results about this complexity measure: Information equals amortized size complexity. We show that the information complexity of randomized decision tree is equal to the logarithm of the amortized worst-case randomized tree size complexity of computing a function f. That is, when computing f on n inputs, the logarithm of the randomized tree size is exactly equal to the amount of information needed to compute the function. Information allows for tree size compression. We show that even when computing f on a single input, the information complexity can be used to compress the size of a tree, if we allow a small loss in success probability. With the recent characterization of Chattopadhyay, Dahiya, Mande, Radhakrishnan, and Sanyal (2023), this result shows that the depth of AND-OR trees can also be compressed in terms of information complexity. Direct Product Theorems. We show that the success-conditioned variant of information complexity satisfies a perfect direct product theorem. This result gives an information complexity analogue of the direct product theorem for success-conditioned randomized query complexity by Ben-David and Blais (2025).
tldr: The paper defines information complexity for randomized decision trees and proves it equals amortized tree size, enables compression, and satisfies a direct product theorem.
motivation: Randomized decision tree complexity lacks an information-theoretic measure analogous to communication complexity, prompting the authors to fill this gap.
method: They define information complexity for randomized decision trees and prove three main theorems using combinatorial and information-theoretic arguments.
result: Information complexity equals the logarithm of amortized worst-case randomized tree size, allows tree size compression with small error, and satisfies a perfect direct product theorem for the success-conditioned variant.
conclusion: This establishes a new complexity measure linking information and decision tree size, with implications for AND-OR tree depth compression and direct product theorems.

title: Parallel Circuit Execution For Scalable Quantum Computation
authors: Avimita Chatterjee, W. Michael Brown, Siyuan Niu, Wibe Albert de Jong, Thomas Lubinski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today's quantum processors have tens to hundreds of physical qubits, but reliable execution of arbitrary circuits remains limited to fewer than 30 entangled qubits across hardware modalities. Building upon prior work, we introduce an error- and topology-aware method for mapping multiple independent circuits onto disjoint regions of a single large-scale QPU for parallel circuit execution. For applications with many similarly sized circuits, such as observable estimation for Hamiltonian simulation, this approach can reduce billed QPU execution time, with ideal speedup proportional to the number of usable partitions. We demonstrate the approach on IBM's 156-qubit ibm_boston processor using standard QED-C benchmark and Hamiltonian-based observable-estimation workloads. Compared with standard sequential execution, parallel execution reduces billed execution time by 3.5-5.5x while retaining 83-92% of the sequential fidelity. We further evaluate the scaling of parallel circuit execution using GPU-accelerated classical simulation, distributing measurement circuits across GPUs via MPI. Using CUDA-Q on the NERSC Perlmutter system, we achieve up to 13.8x speedup on 16 GPUs (86% parallel efficiency) for an H2 electronic-structure simulation, with scaling evaluated across multiple Hamiltonians and circuit counts. These results provide an indication of the performance ceiling that parallel execution on future quantum hardware may eventually approach. Both execution modes are implemented as a runtime option within the QED-C Application-Oriented Benchmark suite. Together, the results show that circuit-level parallelism can reduce execution cost on current quantum hardware and simulation time on GPU clusters, with the potential for greater benefits as device quality and qubit counts increase.
tldr: An error- and topology-aware compilation method maps multiple independent quantum circuits onto disjoint regions of a single large QPU to enable parallel circuit execution, reducing billed execution time on hardware and simulation time on GPU clusters.
motivation: Reliable execution of arbitrary circuits is limited to fewer than 30 entangled qubits, so many workloads (e.g., observable estimation for Hamiltonian simulation) waste most of a large device; running independent circuits in parallel can amortize expensive QPU time.
method: The authors partition a large-scale QPU into disjoint regions using error- and topology-aware mapping, then execute independent circuits concurrently; they also distribute measurement circuits across GPUs with MPI/CUDA-Q for classical simulation scaling.
result: On IBM's 156-qubit ibm_boston they achieve 3.5-5.5x reduction in billed execution time while retaining 83-92% of sequential fidelity, and on NERSC Perlmutter they reach up to 13.8x speedup across 16 GPUs (86% parallel efficiency) for an H2 electronic-structure simulation.
conclusion: Circuit-level parallelism reduces execution cost on current hardware and simulation time on GPU clusters, with expected larger benefits as device quality and qubit counts improve; the approach is integrated as a runtime option in the QED-C benchmark suite.

title: Factoring Six-digit Integers With Superconducting Quantum Circuits
authors: Xi Zhang, Xinsheng Tan, Yang Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integer factorization is a central computational problem with important applications in public-key cryptography. Here, we demonstrate a quantum factorization protocol using a superconducting circuit. Microwave drives are used to engineer a highly tunable effective two-level Hamiltonian whose eigenvalues can be measured spectroscopically. The target integer \(N\) and each candidate factor pair (\(p\),\(q\)) are encoded into the amplitudes, frequencies, and phases of the applied microwave fields. By scanning the candidate pairs while monitoring the spectral response at zero energy, we identify the factor pairs of integers up to six digits. The protocol requires neither two-qubit gates nor quantum entanglement. Its performance is currently limited by the precision of microwave control and the finite linewidth of the spectroscopic response. Improved control accuracy and longer coherence times would extend the accessible range of integers.
tldr: The paper demonstrates integer factorization of up to six-digit numbers using a superconducting circuit by encoding candidate factor pairs into microwave drive parameters and detecting zero-energy spectral response.
motivation: Integer factorization is central to public-key cryptography, and quantum factoring could threaten RSA, but current implementations require complex gates and entanglement.
method: They engineer a highly tunable effective two-level Hamiltonian via microwave drives, encode the target integer and each candidate factor pair into amplitudes, frequencies, and phases, and spectroscopically scan for a zero-energy response to identify factors.
result: They successfully factor integers up to six digits without two-qubit gates or entanglement, with performance limited by microwave control precision and the finite linewidth of the spectroscopic response.
conclusion: The protocol offers a simpler route to quantum factorization, but improved control accuracy and longer coherence times are needed to extend the accessible range, and it currently does not surpass classical methods.

title: Gauge Rigidity And Holonomy Classification Of Time-Scaled Intertwining Cocycles On Hilbert Bundles
authors: Anton Alexa
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the discrete gauge rigidity of time-scaled intertwining cocycles to operator networks over a connected manifold M and classify the holonomy that the continuous setting admits. For dissipative semigroups [MATH] linked by transport operators [MATH] along paths [MATH], we prove that the scaling field carries no monodromy: [MATH] for a continuous positive function [MATH], unique up to a multiplicative constant, with multiplicativity forced by the intertwining relation rather than assumed. For regular cocycles the transport defines a bounded operator connection on a Hilbert bundle over M; the holonomy of a closed loop is confined to the commutant of the generator and decomposes into spectral sectors, on each of which it is adiabatic (Berry-Wilczek-Zee) transport twisted by an independent commutant-valued sector potential; for flat unitary cocycles the holonomy is classified by unitary representations of [MATH] in the commutant. An explicit rotating network over [MATH] exhibits holonomy equal to the parity operator while the Berry connection one-form of every level vanishes identically: the monodromy is carried by [MATH] orientation classes of Moebius eigenline bundles.
tldr: The paper extends gauge rigidity of time-scaled intertwining cocycles to operator networks on Hilbert bundles and classifies the resulting structures, but it is not directly relevant to the research direction.

title: Benchmarking The Computational Power Of Quantum Computers
authors: Timothy Proctor, Oliver Hart, Oliver Widzowski Maupin, Matthew Girling, Daniel Hothem, Daniel Mills, Jordan Hines, Karl Mayer, Jacob S. Nelson, Tyler Leblond, Zohim Chandani, Diego Forlivesi, Piper C. Wysocki, Boldizs\'ar Po\'or, Joan M. Dreiling, Annie Park, Adam P. Reed, Brian Estey, Cameron Foltz, Akhil Isanaka, M. S. Allman, Michael Mills, Maxwell D. Urmey, Peter E. Siegfried, Audrey Faricy, Jin-Sung Kim, Cristina C\^irstoiu, Andrew D. Baczewski, Charles H. Baldwin, Robin Blume-Kohout
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing hardware is advancing rapidly toward utility-scale machines that will enable scientific breakthroughs. Many teams are pursuing distinct and difficult-to-compare routes to this goal, using different qubit technologies and logical architectures. Tracking progress toward quantum utility therefore requires rigorous benchmarks that measure computational capability relative to utility-scale challenge problems and enable fair comparison across disparate platforms. Here we demonstrate direct, cross-platform measurement of quantum computational capability using a new benchmark that quantifies the size of the largest computationally relevant quantum circuits that a machine can execute successfully and the speed at which it can execute them. We apply this quantum universal operation performance system (QUOPS) experimentally to leading processors from Quantinuum, Google, and IBM, computing directly on physical qubits. Translating state-of-the-art resource requirements for recognized challenge problems that represent useful quantum computation into effective QUOPS circuit sizes shows that computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude, motivating fault-tolerant approaches. We use the same benchmark to assess the performance of a simple fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor implemented on up to eight [[7,1,3]]-encoded logical qubits using Quantinuum Helios-1, and project the growth of capability across successive generations of fault-tolerant quantum computers to show how QUOPS can track progress toward quantum scientific utility.
tldr: The paper introduces QUOPS, a cross-platform benchmark that measures the largest computationally relevant quantum circuits a machine can execute and the speed of execution, applied to Quantinuum, Google, and IBM processors.
motivation: Rapid advances in quantum hardware and disparate platform designs make it difficult to compare progress toward quantum utility, necessitating rigorous and fair benchmarks of computational capability.
method: The authors define the quantum universal operation performance system (QUOPS) and experimentally apply it to leading physical-qubit processors and a small fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor using up to eight [[7,1,3]]-encoded qubits on Quantinuum Helios-1.
result: They find that current computational capability must grow by about five orders of magnitude to reach recognized utility-scale challenge problems, and they project capability growth across future fault-tolerant generations.
conclusion: QUOPS provides a platform-independent way to track progress toward quantum scientific utility and motivates fault-tolerant approaches.

title: Path-Degenerate Quantum Interferometry For Decoherence Mitigation In Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Jonas Rittmeyer, Niels Boettner, Farid Khalili, Mikhail Korobko, Roman Schnabel
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical decoherence degrades quantum correlations in squeezed states of light, severely limiting the quantum-nondemolition (QND) sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors. Here, we propose the path-degenerate quantum interferometry scheme that obviates the need for entire optical subsystems---including additional filter cavities, auxiliary parametric amplifiers, and Faraday isolators---thereby drastically reducing spatial mode mismatches while inherently integrating variational output, a long-standing theoretical proposal to further deepen the QND regime. We experimentally demonstrate a core aspect of this scheme, achieving a shot-noise-preserving signal enhancement that directly counteracts the detrimental effects of readout loss. By delivering an improved signal-to-quantum-noise ratio solely through the consolidation and reduction of currently considered optical subsystems, our approach offers a highly optimized route toward enhanced quantum-noise reduction in upcoming LIGO upgrades and next-generation gravitational-wave observatories.
tldr: Proposes a path-degenerate quantum interferometry scheme to mitigate optical decoherence in squeezed-light gravitational-wave detectors, experimentally demonstrating shot-noise-preserving signal enhancement.
motivation: Optical decoherence degrades squeezed states of light and limits quantum-nondemolition sensitivity in gravitational-wave detectors, while existing mitigation schemes require complex optical subsystems that introduce mode mismatches.
method: The scheme consolidates and reduces optical subsystems by eliminating additional filter cavities, auxiliary parametric amplifiers, and Faraday isolators, while integrating variational output; a core aspect is experimentally demonstrated.
result: Achieves shot-noise-preserving signal enhancement that directly counteracts readout loss, improving the signal-to-quantum-noise ratio.
conclusion: Offers a streamlined and optimized route toward enhanced quantum-noise reduction for upcoming LIGO upgrades and next-generation gravitational-wave observatories.

title: Large $n$ Expansions Of The Partition Function For Coulomb Systems On The Surface Of A Cylinder
authors: Peter J. Forrester Bo-Jian Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The two-dimensional one-component plasma forms a droplet in the case that the one-body potential is proportional to the number of charges. Our interest is in studying the large [MATH] form of the corresponding partition function, with the plasma confined to the surface of the cylinder. The one-body potential is (up to technical restrictions) allowed to be arbitrary in the direction of the axis of the cylinder, whereas the coupling is restricted to the exactly solvable value [MATH]. It is demonstrated that a change of variables can be made to an annular droplet plasma model, up to a certain Jacobian factor. The latter can be interpreted as the characteristic function of a certain linear statistic, which generalises the original aim of our study to also analysing the large [MATH] form of the characteristic function for the annular droplet plasma model. While this is well known in the case of soft wall boundary conditions, our analysis (based on Laplace's method applied to certain integrals, and the Euler-Maclaurin summation formula) covers the case of one or two hard walls at the boundary, or inside, of the droplet for which the soft edge formulas are shown to no longer hold. Use of this to study the large [MATH] expansion of the cylinder partition function requires knowledge of the same expansion in the annular case. This is not available in the case of two hard walls inside the droplet, which we treat instead via a direct analysis. In distinction to the case of the annular partition function, the large [MATH] expansion of the logarithm of the cylinder partition function is found to always have no term proportional to [MATH], independent of the presence of hard walls.
tldr: The paper derives large n expansions of the partition function for a two-dimensional one-component plasma on a cylinder surface, mapping it to an annular droplet model and analyzing the breakdown of soft-edge formulas for hard walls.
motivation: Understanding the asymptotic behavior of Coulomb systems in confined geometries is a fundamental problem in mathematical physics, particularly when hard walls replace soft-wall boundary conditions and standard edge scaling fails.
method: The authors use a change of variables to relate the cylinder partition function to an annular droplet plasma model, then apply Laplace's method and the Euler-Maclaurin summation formula to compute large n expansions, treating hard-wall cases both via the annular mapping and direct analysis.
result: The logarithmic large n expansion of the cylinder partition function is shown to have no term proportional to n, independent of the presence of hard walls, while for the annular model the soft-edge formulas no longer hold when one or two hard walls are present inside or at the droplet boundary.
conclusion: This work extends the asymptotic analysis of Coulomb gas partition functions to cylindrical confinement with hard walls, providing new results for the annular droplet model and highlighting a qualitative difference from the annular case regarding the absence of an n term.

title: Feedback Capacity Of Stationary Gaussian Channels: An Optimal Schalkwijk-Kailath Scheme
authors: Oron Sabag David Fay
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider channels with additive colored Gaussian noise and noiseless feedback. Kim's seminal work derived a stationary variational characterization of feedback capacity and further asserted that the capacity-achieving stationary input need not contain a feedback-independent Gaussian component. These results led to the construction of a simple coding scheme, based on the Schalkwijk--Kailath (SK) refinement principle, which was shown to be capacity-achieving. A recent note identified a gap in the proof of the feedback-independent component-removal assertion, thereby leaving the optimality of the SK scheme and subsequent results that rely on it incomplete. In this paper, we prove the component-removal assertion for channels with stationary Gaussian noise that has a rational power spectral density. Our proof uses a perturbation analysis of a convex optimization formulation of feedback capacity and, indeed, shows that every optimizer assigns zero power to the feedback-independent component. Using this stronger property, we construct from any optimizer an explicit SK coding scheme that achieves every rate below feedback capacity with doubly-exponentially decaying maximal error probability.
tldr: The paper proves a component-removal assertion for feedback capacity of stationary Gaussian channels with rational power spectral density and constructs an explicit Schalkwijk-Kailath coding scheme achieving capacity with doubly-exponentially decaying error probability.
motivation: Kim's stationary variational characterization of feedback capacity and the Schalkwijk-Kailath scheme were incomplete due to a gap in the proof of the feedback-independent component-removal assertion, leaving the scheme's optimality unproven.
method: The authors perform a perturbation analysis of a convex optimization formulation of feedback capacity for stationary Gaussian noise with rational spectral density.
result: They prove that every optimizer assigns zero power to the feedback-independent Gaussian component, and use this stronger property to construct an explicit SK coding scheme that achieves every rate below feedback capacity with doubly-exponentially decaying maximal error probability.
conclusion: This work fixes the gap in Kim's proof and establishes the optimality of the Schalkwijk-Kailath scheme for stationary Gaussian feedback channels with rational spectra.
