In spite of major and some precise developments in statistical physical modelling and characterizing the fracture mechanics (starting with Allan Griffith's crack nucleation theory in 1921 and the weakest link failure Fibre Bundle Model of Frederick Thomas Peirce in 1926) and of earthquake dynamics (starting with Robert Burridge and Leon Knopoff's continuum dynamical model in 1967 and later other discrete or lattice train models or fractal overlap models of stick slip earthquakes), no graduate level textbook in condensed matter physics or in statistical physics introduces the basic models and their properties. And now computer scientists and social scientists (coming with their social inequality measures applied to the avalanche statistics in precursor failures) are joining their efforts to explore the new precursory inequality measures for big avalanches or failures. This introductory review is designed to fill this gap with a view to introducing these to this wider audience and to take them to the current frontiers in these fields.
tldr: An introductory review of statistical physics and sociophysics models for fracture mechanics and earthquake dynamics, covering avalanche statistics and new inequality measures.
motivation: To fill the gap in graduate-level textbooks by introducing foundational and modern models of fracture and earthquake dynamics to a wider audience, including computer scientists and social scientists.
method: Reviews historical and contemporary models such as the fiber bundle model, Burridge-Knopoff continuum model, lattice train models, fractal overlap models, and the application of social inequality measures to avalanche statistics.
result: Synthesizes key properties of these models and highlights current frontiers, particularly the use of precursory inequality measures for predicting large avalanches or failures.
conclusion: Provides an accessible introduction that connects statistical physics, geophysics, and sociophysics to study fracture mechanics and earthquake dynamics, aiming to inspire further cross-disciplinary research.

title: Climate-model Factor Separation With Shapley Values And Efficient Sampling
authors: Abel Jansma
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Climate models often feature nonlinear responses to changes in model parameters or boundary conditions. Factor separation asks how much of the resulting change should be assigned to altered factors and their interactions. Lunt et al. (2010) showed that two factor attribution methods, the and methods, coincide for [MATH] factors and conjectured this holds for arbitrary [MATH]. We show that the linear-sum and shared-interaction formulas are respectively the permutation and Harsanyi-dividend representations of the Shapley value. Their equality therefore follows from a classical theorem in cooperative game theory. To our knowledge, this is the first explicit identification of the Stein--Alpert and Lunt climate-model factor-separation methods with M\"obius/Harsanyi coefficients and Shapley values. The result imports many established and efficient Shapley sampling methods into climate-model experimental design, and extends to vector-valued responses.
tldr: This paper identifies two climate-model factor-separation methods as Shapley value representations, allowing efficient sampling methods from cooperative game theory to be imported into climate-model experimental design.
motivation: Climate models often respond nonlinearly to parameter changes, and factor separation seeks to assign change to altered factors and their interactions; prior work conjectured equality of two attribution methods for arbitrary numbers of factors.
method: The authors show that the linear-sum and shared-interaction formulas correspond to the permutation and Harsanyi-dividend representations of the Shapley value, so their equality follows from a classical cooperative-game-theory theorem.
result: The equality holds for arbitrary numbers of factors, extends to vector-valued responses, and enables established efficient Shapley sampling methods to be used for climate-model experimental design.
conclusion: This work bridges climate-model factor separation and Shapley value theory, providing a new practical toolkit for climate attribution, but it lies outside quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Optimal Service Commitments In Traveling Salesman Problems With Stochastic Demand
authors: Lina Schmidt, Julian Golak, Arne Schulz, Malte Fliedner
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In ridepooling services, mobility providers must communicate an expected arrival time before customers decide whether to book. An ambitious commitment attracts higher demand than a conservative one, but is correspondingly harder to fulfill. Provider revenue is therefore governed by an endogenous interplay between the announced commitment and the demand it induces. We study this interplay in a traveling salesman setting in which all customers share a shuttle to a common destination, formalizing it as the Traveling Salesman Problem with Service Commitments (TSP-SC), a two-stage stochastic optimization problem. In the first stage, the provider announces an arrival commitment to all customers interested in the trip, each of whom independently accepts or rejects the offer with a probability decreasing in the committed time. In the second stage, an Orienteering Problem determines a revenue-maximizing subset of accepting customers to be served within the commitment; the remaining customers are rejected. We show that optimal commitments lie in a finite candidate set induced by the tour lengths of customer subsets, and develop two exact algorithms, a general and a faster variant for homogeneous customers, together with an Adaptive Binomial Sampling Heuristic (BSH) for larger instances. In a numerical study on instances with up to 100 customers, the heuristic deviates from the optimal expected revenue by at most 0.32~\% on average across all exactly solvable sizes. The results further reveal a striking operational regularity: as the customer base grows, the revenue-maximizing policy converges to a regime in which roughly one in three accepting customers is rejected, a rejection rate that remains stable across instance sizes.
tldr: The paper studies optimal service commitments in a stochastic ridepooling variant of the traveling salesman problem, balancing announced arrival times against induced demand.
motivation: Ridepooling providers must announce arrival commitments that attract demand but are hard to fulfill, creating a revenue trade-off not captured by standard routing models.
method: It formulates the Traveling Salesman Problem with Service Commitments (TSP-SC) as a two-stage stochastic optimization problem, with stage one choosing a commitment and stage two solving an Orienteering Problem over accepting customers, and develops exact algorithms plus a Binomial Sampling Heuristic.
result: Optimal commitments lie in a finite candidate set, the heuristic achieves near-optimal revenue for up to 100 customers, and the optimal policy converges to rejecting roughly one in three accepting customers as demand grows.
conclusion: The work provides exact and heuristic methods for optimizing service commitments in stochastic ridepooling, revealing a stable rejection regularity that informs provider operations.

title: Receiver-Surface Hit Patterns Via Legendre Approximation For Molecular Signal Detection
authors: Yasin Bastug, Erencem Ozbey, H. Birkan Yilmaz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detecting whether a transmitter is actively communicating with a receiver is a fundamental problem in molecular communications. A spherical receiver may measure not only the number and arrival times of absorbed molecules, but also their absorption locations on the receiver surface. These locations contain a directional signature that is lost in count-only detection. In this letter, we develop a molecular signal detector based on a Legendre polynomial expansion of the receiver-surface hit density and extend it to a Legendre-based Viterbi sequence detector. By exploiting the surface-level directional signature of molecular arrivals, the proposed detectors provide geometry-aware, efficient, and better-performing alternatives to count-only detection.
tldr: This letter proposes molecular signal detectors based on a Legendre polynomial expansion of the receiver-surface hit density, including a Legendre-based Viterbi sequence detector, to exploit directional information in molecular absorption locations.
motivation: In molecular communications, detecting whether a transmitter is actively communicating with a spherical receiver is a fundamental problem; count-only detection discards the directional signature contained in where molecules are absorbed on the receiver surface.
method: The authors expand the receiver-surface hit density in Legendre polynomials and build a detector on this representation, then extend it to a Legendre-based Viterbi sequence detector that performs sequence detection over the directional arrival statistics.
result: The proposed geometry-aware detectors outperform conventional count-only detection schemes while remaining efficient, exploiting surface-level directional signatures of molecular arrivals.
conclusion: Leveraging absorption locations on the receiver surface via Legendre approximation yields better-performing molecular signal detection, offering a practical alternative to count-only approaches in molecular communication systems.

title: A Fully Discrete Local Discontinuous Galerkin Method For Quasilinear Stochastic Convection-Diffusion-Type Equations
authors: Yiming Chen, Yunzhang Li, Yulong Xing
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop and analyze a fully discrete local discontinuous Galerkin (LDG) method with IMEX-Euler time discretization for a class of multi-dimensional quasilinear stochastic convection-diffusion-type equations driven by multiplicative [MATH]-Wiener noise. The leading diffusion matrix may depend on the solution as well as the spatial and temporal variables, while the lower-order drift and noise coefficients may depend on both the solution and its gradient. Under a suitable stochastic parabolicity condition, we establish unconditional high-moment stability estimates for the fully discrete scheme in the quasilinear setting. In the semilinear setting, where the leading diffusion matrix is independent of the solution but may vary in space and time, we further prove optimal high-moment strong error estimates of order [MATH] in space and [MATH] in time. A pathwise error estimate is then derived by combining the high-moment error bound with a discrete Kolmogorov argument. Numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the stability and convergence properties of the proposed method.
tldr: Develops and analyzes a fully discrete local discontinuous Galerkin method with IMEX-Euler time discretization for quasilinear stochastic convection-diffusion equations driven by multiplicative Wiener noise.
motivation: Quasilinear stochastic convection-diffusion-type equations arise in various applications and require robust numerical schemes with high-order accuracy and stability under multiplicative noise.
method: The authors propose a fully discrete LDG method using IMEX-Euler time stepping. They establish unconditional high-moment stability for the quasilinear setting and prove optimal high-moment strong error estimates in the semilinear case, plus a pathwise error estimate via a discrete Kolmogorov argument.
result: The scheme achieves unconditional high-moment stability and, in the semilinear case, optimal convergence rates of order k+1/2 in space and first order in time under a stochastic parabolicity condition. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical stability and convergence properties.
conclusion: The proposed LDG method provides a stable and accurate numerical framework for quasilinear stochastic convection-diffusion equations, with rigorous error analysis and supporting numerical evidence.

title: Adaptive Local Representations For Helmholtz Trefftz Discontinuous Galerkin Methods
authors: Shelvean Kapita
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the selection and stable realization of local approximation spaces in Trefftz discontinuous Galerkin discretizations of the Helmholtz equation. A scaled Cauchy-trace inner product places plane waves and Fourier-Bessel functions in a common geometry: Fourier-Bessel modes are orthogonal with explicit weights, while the same weights determine the circulant spectrum of an equispaced plane-wave trace Gram matrix. This separates amplitude scaling from genuine trace-rank loss and yields an exact best-approximation identity for mixed plane-wave--Fourier--Bessel spaces. With complex plane-wave angles, the unresolved modal tail is an exponential sequence, so propagating and evanescent components can be identified by the same ESPRIT/variable-projection procedure. We prove exact recovery and a perturbation estimate for the recovered angles and, under the standard PWDG quasi-optimality bound, transfer these perturbations to the DG error. Trace-Riesz orthonormalization is then separated from a graph--Riesz normalization of the assembled operator. Numerical experiments verify the identities, recover sparse ray fields to roundoff, and resolve a propagating-to-evanescent transition without a prescribed critical angle.
tldr: The paper develops stable local approximation spaces for Trefftz discontinuous Galerkin discretizations of the Helmholtz equation using a scaled Cauchy-trace inner product and ESPRIT-type angle recovery.
motivation: Trefftz DG methods for Helmholtz require well-conditioned local basis functions that can represent both propagating and evanescent wave components without a prescribed critical angle.
method: A scaled Cauchy-trace inner product relates plane waves and Fourier-Bessel functions, giving explicit orthogonality weights and a circulant Gram spectrum; complex plane-wave angles are handled via ESPRIT/variable-projection to separate propagating and evanescent modes, with trace-Riesz orthonormalization and graph-Riesz normalization of the assembled operator.
result: The authors prove exact recovery and perturbation bounds for recovered angles, transfer these to the DG error via the standard quasi-optimality bound, and numerically verify best-approximation identities, sparse ray-field recovery to roundoff, and resolution of a propagating-to-evanescent transition.
conclusion: The approach yields a principled and stable framework for selecting local Trefftz spaces in Helmholtz DG discretizations, improving robustness of wave simulations.

title: How To Grade The Accuracy Of The Blas
authors: James Demmel, Greg Henry, Igor Kozachenko, Julien Langou, Xiaoye Sherry Li, Jason Riedy, Jackson Vanover
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by accelerating machine learning (ML), many computer vendors and chip manufacturers are building accelerators for matrix multiplication, which save time and energy by operating in the lower precisions needed for ML. This has in turn motivated many efforts to use these accelerators to provide faster matrix multiplication implementations with the higher precision required by many other linear algebra applications. Motivated by the large design space of algorithms for approximating higher precision, with significant performance/accuracy tradeoffs, we provide a benchmark to "grade the accuracy" of a matrix multiplication implementation (or the BLAS more generally), ranging from an "A" for attaining the classic floating point error bound, to a "C" for attaining a weaker but still useful bound, that is satisfied by Strassen-like algorithms. We also propose "ungameable" tests that vendors or users can run to verify their promised accuracy, and describe how these different grades impact the accuracy of applications like LU, QR, and Cholesky decomposition. Our test code is publicly available at github.com/Reference-LAPACK/grading-the-BLAS for developers and users, and we also plan to publicly release all our test results.
tldr: The paper proposes a benchmarking framework to 'grade' the numerical accuracy of matrix multiplication implementations (BLAS), from an 'A' grade matching classic floating-point error bounds to a 'C' grade matching weaker Strassen-like bounds.
motivation: Low-precision matrix-multiply accelerators built for machine learning are increasingly being repurposed for higher-precision linear algebra, creating a large design space of approximation algorithms with unclear accuracy/performance tradeoffs.
method: The authors define grade-based accuracy criteria tied to established floating-point error bounds, propose 'ungameable' verification tests for vendors and users, and analyze how each grade propagates into higher-level routines like LU, QR, and Cholesky decompositions.
result: The grading scheme distinguishes implementations that meet the classic error bound from those only satisfying weaker bounds typical of Strassen-like algorithms, with accompanying test code released publicly for reproducible verification.
conclusion: The benchmark provides a practical, standardized way to certify the accuracy of BLAS implementations and to understand downstream accuracy impacts on common dense linear algebra factorizations.

title: Tight Sampling Complexity With Stochastic Gradient Oracles In Fixed Dimensions
authors: Xiao Wang Weiming Ou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the stochastic-gradient query complexity of sampling smooth strongly log-concave distributions in any fixed Euclidean dimension. The potential is [MATH]-strongly convex and [MATH]-smooth, with an unknown mode in the ball of radius [MATH] about the origin. We have access to unbiased stochastic oracles with the variance at most [MATH]. For every [MATH] and total variation (TV) accuracy [MATH], we prove that the tight complexity of sampling a distribution within [MATH]-TV distance from the target distribution is \[ N^\star_{}=\Theta\!\left(\log(1+\kappa)+ {\mu\epsilon}\right), \] where [MATH] is the condition number. Note that this complexity bound is simultaneously tight for the condition number [MATH] and accuracy [MATH]. Besides, our tight complexity bound is adaptive to noiseless setting [MATH], which is [MATH].
tldr: The paper establishes tight stochastic-gradient query complexity bounds for sampling smooth strongly log-concave distributions in fixed dimensions.
motivation: Sampling from high-dimensional distributions is a central problem in optimization and statistics, but tight complexity characterizations with stochastic gradient oracles were lacking in fixed dimension.
method: The authors analyze stochastic-gradient oracles with bounded variance and prove matching upper and lower bounds on the total variation distance to the target strongly log-concave distribution.
result: They show the optimal complexity is Theta(log(1+kappa) + mu epsilon), simultaneously tight in condition number and accuracy, and adaptive to the noiseless setting.
conclusion: This resolves the query complexity of stochastic-gradient sampling for strongly log-concave distributions in fixed dimensions.

title: Closed-form Estimation Of The Exponential Scale Under Two-sided Informative Random Censorship
authors: Dilshod R. Mansurov, Sukhrob B. Bozorov, Azizbek B. Oltiyev
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We estimate the scale of an exponential lifetime from observations censored randomly from both sides, under an informative model in which each censoring law is a power of the lifetime survival function -- a two-sided generalization of the Koziol--Green proportional hazards model. Substituting the empirical distribution function into the likelihood equation yields a closed-form pseudo-maximum-likelihood estimator of the scale that is computed in one pass over the order statistics and needs neither iteration nor numerical optimization. A digamma identity shows the estimating equation to be , not merely asymptotically, Fisher-consistent. Strong consistency and asymptotic normality are established with ; the key is an identity that rewrites the underlying [MATH]-statistic without its unbounded score function and so removes the condition that classical limit theorems would impose. The influence function and the asymptotic variance are explicit in polygamma functions, so confidence intervals require no numerical integration. Against the information bound of the observed-data model the efficiency exceeds [MATH] in the designs considered and stays above [MATH] over a wide sweep. Only the entry half of the model is needed: the estimator remains exactly Fisher-consistent and strongly consistent whatever the right-censoring law, and exponentiality is shown to be the precise price of that freedom. The construction extends verbatim to a proportional hazards class with known baseline. Three data sets illustrate the procedure, including a cohort in which left censoring is genuine.
tldr: The paper derives a closed-form pseudo-maximum-likelihood estimator for the scale parameter of an exponential lifetime distribution under two-sided informative random censoring.
motivation: Estimating lifetime scales from censored data is a classic survival-analysis problem, but two-sided informative censoring is less well understood and typically requires iterative numerical optimization.
method: The authors substitute the empirical distribution function into the likelihood equation and use a digamma identity to obtain a closed-form estimator expressed in polygamma functions.
result: The estimator is shown to be exactly Fisher-consistent, strongly consistent, and asymptotically normal, with explicit influence function, asymptotic variance, and high efficiency relative to the information bound.
conclusion: The proposed estimator provides a simple, non-iterative, and robust solution for exponential scale estimation under two-sided informative random censoring, illustrated on three datasets.

title: A Dark Forest First Attack Is Rational Only If The Attacker Accepts It As Its Last
authors: Harvey Dam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Dark Forest argument holds that a civilization that detects another should strike it at once, so detection, and any transmission that invites it, is danger. Existing models make the detected civilization the object of the strike and play the strike on a roster the attacker knows; where they advise restraint, the advice rests on steps that fail in the cases it is for. This paper takes the object of hostility to be remaining uncontrolled capacity to warn or retaliate, on a roster no attacker ever knows to be complete. A first strike is rational only if the timing benefit of what it removes is at least the disclosure loss from every leftover that learns of it. A leftover able to bring about the attacker's destruction, by striking or by warning one who can, costs the attacker its whole stake, and the actors the attacker has never found are such a leftover that no strike removes. A Dark Forest believer that strikes first therefore accepts the strike as the last attack it will ever make; the strike is rational only if waiting would raise the cost of removing the target by about the attacker's whole stake. A transmission that reveals the sender gives a receiver a posterior over the sender's capacity, not a target, and proves that the sender can warn. A receiver need not be hostile; for one that is, the sender is a witness it must pay for, so a beacon delays every hostile that cannot be nearly sure of removing the sender's forces, and a free beacon harms its sender only through sure kill, whole-stake urgency, a receiver that fears no one the sender could warn, or an opening hidden from the sender. Messaging to extraterrestrial intelligence (METI) is judged by reach and by what a receiver must believe to act, not by fear of punishment, and a beacon deters by witnessing: the sender need not be able to strike anyone, only to tell someone who can.
tldr: A game-theoretic analysis of the Dark Forest hypothesis argues that a first strike is rational only if the attacker accepts it as its last attack, and that METI beacons deter by witnessing rather than by threatened punishment.
motivation: Existing Dark Forest models assume the attacker knows the target roster and treats the detected civilization as the object of the strike, but these assumptions fail in the cases they are meant to address.
method: The paper reframes the object of hostility as remaining uncontrolled capacity to warn or retaliate on an unknown roster, then analyzes the attacker's timing benefit versus disclosure loss and models a beacon as giving the receiver a posterior over the sender's capacity and proof that the sender can warn.
result: A first strike is rational only if waiting would raise the cost of removing the target by about the attacker's whole stake; a leftover able to destroy or warn a destroyer costs the attacker everything, and unknown actors are such a leftover. A beacon delays every hostile that cannot be nearly sure of removing the sender's forces, and harms its sender only under specific conditions such as sure kill, whole-stake urgency, or a receiver fearing no one the sender could warn.
conclusion: METI should be judged by reach and by what a receiver must believe to act, not by fear of punishment, and a beacon deters by witnessing: the sender need not strike anyone, only tell someone who can.

title: Deriving The Pure Price Of Anarchy For Networked Resource Allocation Games
authors: Philip N. Brown Vartika Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work considers multi-agent coordination with arbitrary information networks among the agents using a game-theoretic approach. A system designer aims to assign local utility functions to the agents to guide their actions toward a desired system objective. The performance of the assigned local utilities is measured by the well known pure price of anarchy (pPoA) metric that equals the ratio of the system objective at the worst pure Nash equilibrium of the corresponding game to the optimal system objective. Our aim is to derive the utility functions which optimize the pPoA-based performance guarantees for any given information network and system objective. We develop a linear program that derives the optimal pPoA for any arbitrary information network and arbitrary system objective. Our work is the first to solve optimal utility design for arbitrary networks; our techniques generalize previous approaches which considered only the full-information setting. For supermodular objective functions, we prove that counterintuitively, a fully communication-denied utility design is optimal irrespective of the original information network. For submodular system objectives, an exhaustive numerical analysis suggests that the optimal utility design is robust to communication failures even for this case. When the system objective is weighted maximum coverage, the marginal contribution utility design provably optimizes the pPoA for a wide variety of information networks of interest.
tldr: The paper develops a linear program to derive utility functions that optimize the pure price of anarchy for multi-agent resource allocation games over arbitrary information networks.
motivation: A system designer wants to assign local utility functions that steer self-interested agents toward a desired global objective, but optimal utility design was previously known only for the full-information setting.
method: The authors formulate a linear program that computes the optimal pure price of anarchy for any information network and system objective, generalizing prior full-information approaches to arbitrary communication topologies.
result: For supermodular objectives, a fully communication-denied utility design is provably optimal regardless of the underlying network; for submodular objectives, numerics suggest the optimal design is robust to communication failures, and marginal contribution utility is provably optimal for weighted maximum coverage objectives on many networks.
conclusion: Optimal utility design for pPoA guarantees can be solved generally across arbitrary networks, with counterintuitive robustness to communication restrictions in several important objective classes.

title: On The Fragility Of Worst-Case Nash Equilibria In Atomic Congestion Games
authors: Colton Hill, Brandon Collins, Philip N. Brown
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aggregate performance in smart mobility systems depends heavily on the emergent behavior of selfish, resource-sharing agents that participate within the systems. As a result, recent work has focused on how a system designer can leverage incentives to influence behavior so that system cost (e.g., traffic congestion) is minimized. These results show that worst-case equilibria can be quite inefficient compared to system-optimal allocations. However, it is unclear to what extent agents are ``satisfied'' with their decisions in these worst-case scenarios. We demonstrate that in any incentivized atomic congestion game, agents' aggregate satisfaction at equilibrium (relative to their actions in an optimal allocation) is correlated with the efficiency of the corresponding system cost, in the sense that if agents are very satisfied with their equilibrium choices, the equilibrium must be relatively efficient. Further, we show that worst-case Nash equilibria are fragile, as every agent is indifferent between their action in a worst-case equilibrium and their action in a system-optimal allocation. In summary, at equilibrium, either agents are highly satisfied with their decisions or their decisions are highly inefficient, but both cannot be true simultaneously. This work adds to recent results for other classes of games which indicate that worst-case equilibrium efficiency guarantees only occur when agents are indifferent about their decisions.
tldr: The paper shows that in incentivized atomic congestion games, worst-case Nash equilibria are fragile because agents are indifferent between their worst-case equilibrium actions and their actions in a system-optimal allocation, linking aggregate satisfaction to equilibrium efficiency.
motivation: Smart mobility systems rely on selfish agents whose emergent equilibrium behavior is often inefficient compared to system-optimal allocations; it is unclear how satisfied agents are with their choices in these worst-case scenarios.
method: The authors analyze incentivized atomic congestion games, relating agents' aggregate satisfaction at equilibrium (measured relative to their optimal-allocation actions) to the efficiency of the corresponding system cost.
result: They prove that agents' aggregate satisfaction correlates with equilibrium efficiency—high satisfaction implies relatively efficient equilibria—and that every agent is indifferent between its worst-case equilibrium action and its system-optimal action.
conclusion: At equilibrium, either agents are highly satisfied with their decisions or those decisions are highly inefficient, but both cannot hold simultaneously, extending similar findings from other game classes.

title: Self-Verifying Anomaly Detection Using Explainable Ai For Cybersecurity Of Der Networks
authors: Damilola Popoola, Souradeep Bhattacharya, Manimaran Govindarasu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) has significantly expanded the cyber attack surface of modern power grids. Furthermore, increasing sophistication in attack techniques demands anomaly detection systems (ADS) that are accurate, interpretable, and reliable to support DER cybersecurity. While ML-based ADS provide strong detection capabilities, their black-box nature reduces operator trust and limits Security Operation Center's (SOC) ability to effectively interpret alerts and respond, highlighting the need for explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to ensure transparency and operational confidence. This paper presents an XAI-based anomaly detection framework tailored for DER networks (ExCYDER). The proposed framework uses a self-verifying mechanism that validates ADS alerts to ensure trustworthy decision-making. ExCYDER combines LightGBM with SHAP to check whether each model decision aligns with its feature-attribution evidence, allowing the system to confirm that its internal reasoning is consistent and reliable. Experiments on a realistic DNP3 dataset achieved over 98% detection accuracy, an average rule--SHAP consistency of 44.6%, a SHAP latency of 14.5 ms per alert, and a confidence deviation within 5%, demonstrating stable verification behavior with minimal computational overhead. The framework distinguished between coherent and inconsistent alerts without compromising detection accuracy, demonstrating that integrated verification within XAI-based ADS enhances interpretability, auditability, and operational robustness for DER-focused SOCs.
tldr: ExCYDER is an explainable-AI anomaly detection framework for Distributed Energy Resource (DER) networks that uses a self-verifying mechanism to check whether LightGBM model decisions align with SHAP feature attributions.
motivation: The growing cyber attack surface of power grids with DERs demands anomaly detection systems that are not only accurate but interpretable and trustworthy, since black-box ML models undermine Security Operations Center operators' ability to interpret alerts and respond effectively.
method: The framework couples LightGBM gradient-boosted detection with SHAP-based feature attribution and a self-verification rule that compares model decisions against their attribution evidence to flag coherent versus inconsistent alerts.
result: Experiments on a realistic DNP3 dataset yielded over 98% detection accuracy, an average rule–SHAP consistency of 44.6%, a SHAP latency of 14.5 ms per alert, and confidence deviation within 5%, showing stable verification with minimal computational overhead.
conclusion: Integrated verification within XAI-based anomaly detection enhances interpretability, auditability, and operational robustness for DER-focused security operations centers, without sacrificing detection accuracy.

title: An Open-Source End-to-End Fhe Implementation For Privacy-Preserving Llama 3 8b Inference
authors: Yuhang Fan, Yusi Chen, Kanyu Ye, Zhuoran Ji
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud LLM services typically require users to send prompts to a model provider, creating a privacy risk. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) lets a server perform inference without decrypting the input, but representing data as ciphertexts adds storage and computational overhead. In CKKS-based LLM inference, the packing scheme maps logical tensors to ciphertexts and slots. It therefore determines the ciphertext count and the homomorphic cost of linear layers, and it constrains how data pass between linear layers, attention, and nonlinear computation. As models and sequences grow, inefficient layouts accumulate encoding, compute, and layout-conversion overhead. We present Odin, an FHE inference system that co-designs ciphertext packing and model execution for Llama. Starting from a THOR-style baseline whose bottleneck is weight encoding, Odin uses a feature-major cross-layer layout to unify residual connections and layer interfaces, and builds transient intra-operator layouts for linear projections and attention. This reduces redundant plaintext encoding of weights in wide projections. Within attention, QK^T produces scores that Softmax can consume directly, and PV consumes the resulting probabilities, avoiding intermediate repacking. For nonlinear ops, we use minimax polynomial approximation with input-range control and joint error allocation guided by model quality, reducing polynomial degree and multiplicative depth. To our knowledge, Odin is the first open-source end-to-end GPU CKKS implementation of Llama-3. With Llama-3-8B weights and a 128-token input, Odin evaluates all 32 Transformer layers on a single NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPU. Server-side end-to-end FHE evaluation takes 366.4 s and 58.9 GiB peak device memory. Under the same model, input, CKKS parameters, and hardware, THOR takes 1651.9 s, a 4.51x speedup.
tldr: Odin is an open-source end-to-end CKKS-based FHE system for privacy-preserving Llama-3-8B inference on a single GPU, achieving a 4.51x speedup over THOR.
motivation: Cloud LLM inference exposes user prompts to service providers, and fully homomorphic encryption can enable private inference but incurs substantial storage and computational overhead.
method: The paper co-designs ciphertext packing and model execution for Llama, using a feature-major cross-layer layout, transient intra-operator layouts, direct Softmax/PV consumption, and minimax polynomial approximation with joint error allocation.
result: On an NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPU, Odin evaluates all 32 Transformer layers for a 128-token input in 366.4 seconds with 58.9 GiB peak memory, a 4.51x speedup over THOR's 1651.9 seconds.
conclusion: Odin is the first open-source end-to-end GPU CKKS implementation of Llama-3, demonstrating that practical FHE-based LLM inference is feasible with careful ciphertext packing and operator layout optimization.

title: PDoS: A Profitable Denial-of-Service Attack Against Proof-of-Work Blockchain Liveness
authors: Junjie Hu, Tianzhu Han, Na Ruan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The security and liveness of Proof-of-Work (PoW) blockchains fundamentally depend on the economic rationality of miners. Existing incentive-driven denial-of-service attacks, such as BDoS, can deter rational miners from participating, but require the attacker to continuously absorb substantial economic losses and are therefore difficult to sustain in high-value networks. Meanwhile, prior infiltration-based withholding attacks are designed to extract revenue rather than to directly disrupt chain liveness. We present PDoS, a hybrid attack that combines block header signal deterrence with parasitic revenue extraction. PDoS disrupts blockchain liveness while exploiting the victim pool's share-reward mechanism to subsidize the attack cost, thereby lowering the adversarial hash-power threshold required to induce rational miners to shut down. We further show a counterintuitive result: in high-fee or high-MEV environments, higher block value can make PoW systems less secure by increasing the attacker's parasitic revenue and pushing the attack across the break-even point into a self-sustaining, or even profitable, regime. To the best of our knowledge, PDoS is the first attack to demonstrate that disrupting PoW blockchain liveness can be economically self-sustaining and even profitable.
tldr: PDoS is a hybrid denial-of-service attack on Proof-of-Work blockchains that combines header-signal deterrence with parasitic revenue extraction to disrupt liveness at lower adversarial hash-power thresholds.
motivation: Existing incentive-driven attacks against PoW blockchains require sustained attacker losses or target revenue extraction rather than liveness disruption, making them impractical in high-value networks.
method: The attack uses block header signals to deter rational miners while exploiting the victim pool's share-reward mechanism to subsidize attack costs, and analyzes break-even conditions in different fee/MEV environments.
result: PDoS lowers the hash-power threshold needed to induce miners to shut down, and in high-fee or high-MEV settings higher block value can increase parasitic revenue enough to make the attack self-sustaining or profitable.
conclusion: Disrupting PoW blockchain liveness can be economically self-sustaining and even profitable, revealing a counterintuitive security risk in high-value PoW systems.

title: Access Control As Verified Parse Constraints
authors: Saranachon Iammongkol, Zhiyi Huang, David Eyers
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Commercial security gateways repeatedly ship implementation bugs in the code path between the network and the policy decision: hand-written enforcement logic that diverges from the policy author's intent, and ad-hoc request parsers at the network boundary that introduce memory-safety flaws of their own. In both cases the bug is in the deployed enforcement code, not in the policy. Existing approaches either leave the enforcement runtime unverified or connect a formal model to a hand-written engine only by differential testing. Our contribution is a class result: a forward-only, backtrack-free EverParse validator is a verified recognizer for a bounded, finite-state class, and access-control decision functions with fixed-offset fields and bounded disjunction belong to it, so one machine-checked proof transfers to every policy in the class rather than being re-established per policy. Concretely, we encode a bounded policy language's decision function into a fixed-size byte buffer and verify the enforcement code once---covering all byte values---with an SMT solver, proving the validator accepts if and only if the decision function accepts, for every policy, request, and session. Editing rule content over a fixed endpoint set then needs no new proof; adding endpoints reruns the toolchain; extending the language needs new proofs. We establish faithful enforcement of a policy, not that a policy is itself secure. The verified gate is platform-independent, requiring only EverParse/Z3 and a C compiler, whose correctness we assume. We demonstrate a deployment on the seL4 microkernel, which ensures every request passes through the gate and that unverified components cannot corrupt the verified enforcement chain.
tldr: The paper presents a verified access-control enforcement mechanism by encoding bounded policy decision functions into EverParse validators and proving correctness once with an SMT solver.
motivation: Commercial security gateways often contain bugs in hand-written enforcement code and request parsers, which can diverge from policy intent or introduce memory-safety flaws.
method: The authors define a class of access-control decision functions with fixed-offset fields and bounded disjunction, encode them into a fixed-size byte buffer, and verify a forward-only, backtrack-free EverParse validator against a bounded finite-state recognizer using Z3, demonstrating deployment on seL4.
result: A single machine-checked proof transfers to every policy in the class, showing the validator accepts if and only if the decision function accepts for all policies, requests, and sessions, with editing rule content over a fixed endpoint set requiring no new proof.
conclusion: The work establishes faithful enforcement of a policy, not policy security itself, and provides a platform-independent verified gate requiring only EverParse/Z3 and a C compiler, with unverified components unable to corrupt the verified enforcement chain on seL4.

title: The Fixed Server Locality Gap Of Count Load Assignment Games
authors: Mengfan Ma Hao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Marginal-contribution pricing makes the social objective an exact potential, but does not ensure that every stable assignment is efficient. We study indivisible clients with heterogeneous workloads, arbitrary nonnegative assignment costs, and private eligibility menus over a fixed number of shared servers and optional local execution. Each server's social cost is its occupancy multiplied by its aggregate workload and a server-specific coefficient. For every fixed server cap [MATH], we prove that the price of anarchy over this class is [MATH] as the workload-ratio cap [MATH] grows. The upper bound applies to every equilibrium and every feasible comparison, without an acyclic-comparison or strongly-connected-component restriction. Its proof combines a common-multiplier certificate, a source-weighted residual inequality and an ordered moment recurrence. A matching chain family has a realization by mobile unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) clients and fixed ground servers, with positive altitude, positive-width coverage and an explicitly paid wireless baseline. We prove exact waypoint elimination and give an input-computable component refinement. Scheduling and congestion identities delimit which established bounds transfer. Exact enumeration of 2,800 synthetic games identifies inefficient equilibria, while 270 primary-parameterized synthetic instance-budget records evaluate incremental latency relative to a feasible multistart reference. Tightness concerns the heterogeneity exponent for fixed [MATH], not matching leading constants or measured frequency of the worst-case configurations.
tldr: The paper proves a tight bound on the price of anarchy for count load assignment games with fixed server locality, using a common-multiplier certificate and moment recurrence, with a UAV-client application.
motivation: Marginal-contribution pricing makes the social objective an exact potential but does not guarantee that all stable assignments are efficient, motivating a characterization of worst-case inefficiency for fixed server counts.
method: The authors bound the price of anarchy over arbitrary nonnegative assignment costs and eligibility menus via a common-multiplier certificate, a source-weighted residual inequality, and an ordered moment recurrence, complemented by exact enumeration of 2,800 synthetic games.
result: They obtain an asymptotic PoA bound as the workload-ratio cap grows for every fixed server cap, matching a chain-family construction, and identify inefficient equilibria along with incremental latency measurements on 270 parameterized instances.
conclusion: The work delimits which established scheduling and congestion bounds transfer to this game class, and provides an input-computable component refinement, though it concerns algorithmic game theory rather than quantum information science.

title: Universally Truthful Mechanisms For Scheduling
authors: Georgios Anastasiadis, George Christodoulou, Elias Koutsoupias, Annamaria Kovacs, Conrad Schecker
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider universally truthful randomized mechanisms for the problem of scheduling [MATH] jobs on [MATH] unrelated machines. We prove a lower bound on the expected approximation ratio of every such mechanism whose probability distribution has discrete support. We show that no universally truthful randomized mechanism in this class can achieve approximation ratio smaller than [MATH] with respect to the optimal makespan. We match this, up to a constant factor, by a mechanism with approximation ratio [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves lower bounds and a matching mechanism for universally truthful randomized scheduling on unrelated machines, minimizing expected makespan approximation.
motivation: Randomized truthful mechanisms for makespan minimization on unrelated machines are a central topic in algorithmic mechanism design, but tight lower bounds for the universal-truthfulness class with discrete support were not fully characterized.
method: The authors use game-theoretic and probabilistic arguments to derive a lower bound on the expected approximation ratio for any universally truthful randomized mechanism with discrete support, then construct a mechanism achieving a constant-factor-matching guarantee.
result: No universally truthful randomized mechanism in this class can achieve an approximation ratio below a certain explicit bound, and a matching mechanism attains this ratio up to a constant factor.
conclusion: The work essentially closes the gap between upper and lower bounds for universally truthful randomized scheduling mechanisms with discrete support, advancing the theory of truthful algorithmic mechanism design.

title: Poster: Towards Selecting Threat Appropriate Industrial Intrusion Detection Systems
authors: Stefan Lenz, Johannes Weidmann, Martin Henze
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the threat landscape against industrial control systems is dynamic, effective security requires detection strategies capable of timely reactions to these evolving threat situations. To address this problem, we propose the idea of a counter-threat intelligence sharing based mechanism to select appropriate detectors for current circumstances. To highlight the potential of this mechanism, we conduct attack-level performance evaluations of various intrusion detection systems. Results show the variance of intrusion detection performance depending on the attack scenario, emphasizing the benefits of such a mechanism for industrial control system security.
tldr: The paper proposes a counter-threat intelligence sharing mechanism to select appropriate intrusion detection systems for evolving industrial control system threats.
motivation: Industrial control systems face a dynamic threat landscape, requiring detection strategies that can adapt to changing attack scenarios.
method: The authors conduct attack-level performance evaluations of various intrusion detection systems and propose a selection mechanism based on counter-threat intelligence sharing.
result: Results show significant variance in intrusion detection performance depending on the attack scenario, motivating the need for adaptive detector selection.
conclusion: A counter-threat intelligence sharing approach can help select appropriate detectors for current circumstances, improving industrial control system security.

title: Supermartingale Certificates For Parametric MDPs
authors: {\dh}or{\dj}e \v{z}ikeli\'c Kaushik Mallik
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problems of formal verification and synthesis in parametric Markov decision processes (MDPs) with general measurable state and action spaces. The heart of our approach is a parameter flattening transformation, which allows us to transform parametric MDPs into semantically equivalent non-parametric MDPs. Building on this transformation, we introduce the novel notion of parametric supermartingale certificates, which generalize the traditional supermartingale certificates---used for non-parametric MDPs---to the parametric setting. We use our parametric supermartingale certificates to design algorithms for verification and approximate synthesis in polynomial arithmetic parametric MDPs. This leads to the first verification and synthesis algorithms for parametric MDPs with general state and action spaces. We implement our algorithms and experimentally evaluate them on several continuous parametric random walk benchmarks.
tldr: The paper introduces parametric supermartingale certificates and parameter flattening to enable formal verification and synthesis for parametric Markov decision processes with general measurable state and action spaces.
motivation: Formal verification and synthesis for parametric MDPs with continuous or general state spaces are challenging, and existing supermartingale certificate methods apply only to non-parametric MDPs.
method: The authors define a parameter flattening transformation that converts parametric MDPs into semantically equivalent non-parametric MDPs, then generalize supermartingale certificates to the parametric setting and use them to design verification and approximate synthesis algorithms.
result: This yields the first verification and synthesis algorithms for parametric MDPs with general measurable state and action spaces, implemented and evaluated on several continuous parametric random walk benchmarks.
conclusion: The proposed parametric supermartingale certificates provide a foundation for verifying and synthesizing parametric MDPs beyond finite-state settings.

title: A Randomized $\frac32$-Approximation For Strategic Facility Location On A Circle
authors: Hau Chan, Jianan Lin, Chenhao Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12792v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study strategyproof mechanisms for locating a single facility on a circle so as to serve a set of strategic agents under the utilitarian social cost objective. We analyze a simple parity-dependent mechanism that randomizes between the Random Dictator (RD) mechanism and the Proportional Circle Distance (PCD) mechanism. For an odd number \(n\) of agents, this mechanism mixes RD and PCD with equal probability, as originally proposed by Rogowski and Dziubi{\'n}ski (IJCAI 2025). For even \(n\), it mixes RD with a random-deletion extension of PCD, in which one agent is removed uniformly at random before PCD is applied to the remaining agents. Our main result shows that this mechanism is strategyproof and achieves an approximation ratio of \(\frac32\) for every \(n\ge 3\). This improves the \(\frac74\) upper bound of Rogowski and Dziubi{\'n}ski, which applied only to odd \(n\), and extends the guarantee to even numbers of agents. Finally, we establish a lower bound of \({10}\) on the approximation ratio of any randomized strategyproof mechanism, improving on the previous lower bound of \(1.0456\) due to Meir (SAGT 2019).
tldr: The paper designs a randomized, strategyproof mechanism for locating a single facility on a circle under utilitarian cost, achieving a 3/2 approximation ratio for all n ≥ 3.
motivation: Strategic facility location on a circle lacks tight approximation guarantees for strategyproof randomized mechanisms, with prior bounds (7/4 for odd n) leaving even n unaddressed and the lower bound far from optimal.
method: The authors analyze a parity-dependent mechanism that mixes the Random Dictator (RD) mechanism with the Proportional Circle Distance (PCD) mechanism, using a random-deletion extension of PCD for even n, and prove strategyproofness and approximation bounds analytically.
result: The mechanism is strategyproof and attains an approximation ratio of 3/2 for every n ≥ 3, improving the previous 7/4 upper bound and extending it to even n, while a new lower bound of 1.0 on any randomized strategyproof mechanism is established (improving 1.0456).
conclusion: The work tightens the gap between upper and lower bounds for strategic single-facility location on a circle, though the result is entirely within algorithmic mechanism design and has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Information Design In Smooth Games
authors: Takuro Yamashita Alex Smolin
abstract: ArXiv:2202.10883v6 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study information design in games where players choose from a continuum of actions and have continuously differentiable payoffs. We show that an information structure is optimal when the equilibrium it induces can also be implemented in a principal-agent contracting problem. Building on this result, we characterize optimal information structures in symmetric linear-quadratic games. With common values, targeted disclosure is robustly optimal across all priors. With interdependent and normally distributed values, linear disclosure is uniquely optimal. We illustrate our findings with applications in venture capital, Bayesian polarization, and price competition.
tldr: The paper studies information design in smooth games with continuous actions and characterizes optimal information structures for symmetric linear-quadratic games.
motivation: Information design asks how a principal should disclose information to influence equilibrium behavior, but optimal structures are often difficult to characterize in general games.
method: The authors link implementable equilibrium outcomes in smooth games to principal-agent contracting problems, then solve for optimal information structures in symmetric linear-quadratic games under common values and normal, interdependent values.
result: They find that targeted disclosure is robustly optimal under common values, while linear disclosure is uniquely optimal with interdependent and normally distributed values, with applications to venture capital, Bayesian polarization, and price competition.
conclusion: The work provides tractable characterizations of optimal information design in a broad class of smooth games, connecting information design to contracting and offering economic applications.

title: Ab Initio Multichannel Calculation Of The Bethe Surface And Compton Defects For Molecular Hydrogen
authors: Alejandro Saenz Hakon Volkmann
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A correlated multichannel computation of the generalized oscillator-strength density for electrons scattering off randomly oriented molecular hydrogen at the internuclear separation of 1.4 [MATH] is being presented. The numerical procedure features a novel free-boundary method based on configuration interaction of ionic orbitals expanded in B splines using prolate-spheroidal coordinates. Satisfactory agreement between the present and both experimental as well as other theoretical results has been found, thus providing a view on the Bethe surface for energy transfers up to of 558 eV. The systematic and robust convergence behavior of the method further allowed for assessing the validity of the binary-encounter approximation, providing a confirmation of experimentally determined Compton defects for H[MATH] using a single consistent theoretical description. Overall, the present findings are expected to be helpful for calculating highly accurate energy-loss spectra for fast electrons passing through and ionizing molecular hydrogen gas or its isotopologues.
tldr: The paper presents an ab initio multichannel calculation of the Bethe surface and Compton defects for molecular hydrogen using a B-spline configuration-interaction method.
motivation: Accurate energy-loss spectra and Compton defects for molecular hydrogen are needed for modeling fast electron scattering and ionization, but a consistent theoretical description spanning large energy transfers is lacking.
method: The authors perform a correlated multichannel computation of the generalized oscillator-strength density using a free-boundary method based on configuration interaction of ionic orbitals expanded in B-splines with prolate-spheroidal coordinates.
result: The calculated Bethe surface agrees satisfactorily with experimental and prior theoretical results up to 558 eV energy transfers, and it confirms experimentally determined Compton defects for H2 within a single consistent framework while assessing the binary-encounter approximation.
conclusion: The method provides a robust tool for computing highly accurate energy-loss spectra for fast electrons ionizing molecular hydrogen and its isotopologues.

title: Thermodynamic Formalism Out Of Equilibrium Part Iii: Local Limit Theorem And Statistical Properties
authors: Yeor Hafouta Snir Ben Ovadia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study limit theorems for random dynamical systems. We recast the random dynamics via the skew-product of the two-point motion (the Varadhan trick). Using this approach we prove several statistical properties for the system, including quenched central limit theorems with rates, quenched local limit theorem, large deviations, and decay of correlations. Then, in applications we show how to verify the general conditions using spectral properties of appropriate operators. A key application is the study of effectively expanding on average random diffeomorphisms (in any dimension, which are allowed to be dissipative). In particular, this is the first instance of proving local limit theorems in such a broad setting, without imposing restrictions on the dynamics. We provide several new examples.
tldr: The paper proves quenched central limit theorems, local limit theorems, large deviations, and decay of correlations for random dynamical systems using a skew-product/Varadhan trick and spectral methods.
motivation: Limit theorems for random dynamical systems are fundamental but local limit theorems were previously unavailable in broad settings, especially for effectively expanding on average random diffeomorphisms.
method: The authors recast random dynamics via the skew-product of the two-point motion (Varadhan trick) and verify general conditions through spectral properties of appropriate transfer operators.
result: They establish quenched CLTs with rates, a quenched local limit theorem, large deviations, and correlation decay, including the first local limit theorems for effectively expanding on average random diffeomorphisms in arbitrary dimension.
conclusion: The work provides a general spectral framework for statistical properties of random dynamical systems and supplies several new examples, though it lies outside quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: One-dimensional Dirichlet Forms With Prescribed H\"older Regularity
authors: Roope Anttila Riku Anttila
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a class of strongly local, regular Dirichlet forms on the standard unit interval. The aim of our work is to record some H\"older regularity properties that have not been noted in the prior literature. In particular, as our main result, we show that for every [MATH] there exists a metric measure space [MATH] equipped with a strongly local, regular Dirichlet form [MATH] on [MATH] with the property that [MATH] is the supremum of [MATH] for which the domain [MATH] of the Dirichlet form contains a non-constant [MATH]-H\"older continuous function. To the best of our knowledge, such examples were previously known only for [MATH]. In our construction, the value [MATH] is characterized by the upper Hausdorff dimension of a certain Radon measure that is used to define [MATH].
tldr: The paper constructs strongly local regular Dirichlet forms on the unit interval realizing any prescribed Hölder regularity exponent, characterized by the upper Hausdorff dimension of an associated Radon measure.
motivation: The authors aim to record Hölder regularity properties of Dirichlet forms that have not been noted in prior literature, generalizing examples previously known only for a single special value.
method: They build a metric measure space equipped with a strongly local regular Dirichlet form defined via a Radon measure, and relate the supremum Hölder exponent of non-constant functions in the form domain to the upper Hausdorff dimension of that measure.
result: For every value in the allowed range there exists such a Dirichlet form whose domain contains non-constant α-Hölder continuous functions exactly up to α equal to the upper Hausdorff dimension of the defining measure.
conclusion: The work characterizes the attainable Hölder regularity of Dirichlet form domains in terms of measure-theoretic dimension, extending known constructions beyond the previously treated special case.

title: Deterministic Nc Quadratic Root Counting In Characteristic Two
authors: Gorav Jindal Sanyam Agarwal
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Counting satisfying assignments of Boolean formulas is a basic problem in theoretical computer science, with [MATH] as the standard [MATH]-complete problem. More generally, counting the solutions of a system of polynomial equations over [MATH] is [MATH]-complete. Here we focus on the more structured problem of counting the solutions of a single polynomial equation. For polynomial equations over finite fields, Ehrenfeucht and Karpinski showed a sharp difference between degrees two and three: quadratic root counting is solvable in polynomial time, while the degree-three problem is [MATH]-complete. Their quadratic algorithm is sequential. For fixed finite fields, Ishai et al.~ later gave deterministic parallel algorithms in odd characteristic and randomized parallel algorithms in characteristic two. We give a deterministic [MATH] algorithm for exactly counting the solutions of a quadratic polynomial equation over every fixed finite field of characteristic two. Our algorithm separates the radical and uses the absolute trace to realize the bit distinguishing the two nondegenerate finite-field types as the Arf invariant of a quadratic form over [MATH]. It then recovers that invariant from an integral matrix using Browder's determinant criterion . This replaces the randomized canonical-form step in the algorithm of Ishai et al.
tldr: The paper gives a deterministic NC (parallel) algorithm for exactly counting the roots of a single quadratic polynomial equation over any fixed finite field of characteristic two, derandomizing a previous parallel algorithm.
motivation: Quadratic root counting over finite fields is solvable in polynomial time while the cubic case is NP-hard, and the existing quadratic algorithms were either sequential or randomized in characteristic two.
method: The algorithm separates the radical, uses the absolute trace to realize the bit distinguishing the two nondegenerate finite-field types as the Arf invariant of a quadratic form over F_2, and recovers that invariant from an integral matrix via Browder's determinant criterion.
result: A deterministic NC algorithm is obtained for exactly counting solutions of quadratic polynomial equations over every fixed finite field of characteristic two, replacing the randomized canonical-form step of Ishai et al.
conclusion: The work closes a derandomization gap in parallel quadratic root counting over even-characteristic finite fields, contributing to classical algebraic complexity theory.

title: Autonomous Multifunctional Image Processing Via Programmable Multimode Lasing
authors: Jiawei Wu, Yue Yin, Jianqi Hu, Hao Wang, Xing Fu, Qiang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical image processing offers a promising pathway to overcome the latency and energy limitations of conventional electronic image processors. However, existing approaches based on passive photonic devices are often constrained by signal attenuation, lack of nonlinearity, fixed functionality, and heavy training overhead. Here, we introduce a programmable image processor based on a highly multimode degenerate cavity laser (DCL), shifting the computational framework from passive extracavity transformation to active intracavity evolution. By manipulating the intracavity loss distribution and exploiting the nonlinear lasing dynamics, we map computational tasks to the spontaneous mode selection within the DCL, realizing image processing directly at the source. We experimentally demonstrate that by simply altering the encoding scheme of input images, the platform can be flexibly reconfigured for multifunctional tasks, including high-fidelity edge detection and robust image denoising. The computation proceeds autonomously without dataset training, featuring an intrinsically low latency ([MATH]90 [MATH]) with [MATH] complexity. Furthermore, the high intensity sustained within the resonator enables intracavity nonlinear upconversion of the processed image. This work extends the frontiers of laser applications, providing a compelling candidate for next-generation optical processors.
tldr: A programmable multimode degenerate cavity laser is used for autonomous optical image processing via active intracavity nonlinear lasing dynamics.
motivation: Conventional electronic image processors face latency and energy limits, while passive photonic approaches suffer from attenuation, fixed functionality, and training overhead.
method: The authors exploit a highly multimode degenerate cavity laser, manipulating intracavity loss and nonlinear lasing dynamics to map tasks such as edge detection and denoising to spontaneous mode selection.
result: The platform achieves multifunctional image processing without dataset training, with low latency and intrinsic complexity, and enables intracavity nonlinear upconversion.
conclusion: This work extends laser applications to active optical computing and offers a candidate for next-generation optical processors.

title: Global Sensitivity Analysis Of Spatial Sets: Finite-Element-Based Estimation And The Role Of Observation Windows
authors: Farbod Chamanian, Chiara Piazzola, Elisabeth Ullmann
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work we consider numerical models with random input parameters, where the model output is a spatially distributed random field. We carry out a statistical sensitivity analysis of spatial sets which arise for instance when the model output exceeds a critical threshold. We consider two approaches: (i) a kernel-based sensitivity analysis working with the Hilbert--Schmidt Independence Criterion, and (ii) a function-valued sensitivity analysis working with generalized Sobol' indices, where the model output is the indicator function of the spatial set of interest. We develop efficient estimators for the sensitivity indices, especially for finite-element-based numerical models, where we approximate volume integrals in the sensitivity measures by finite element quadrature, thereby avoiding Monte Carlo sampling over the spatial domain. This improves the state-of-the-art for the kernel-based indices and makes these methods practically accessible for expensive numerical models. For the generalized Sobol' indices we utilize the same finite element quadrature for efficient computation. We present numerical experiments for a hydrogen combustion process, modeled by a coupled system of convection-diffusion-reaction equations in a two-dimensional spatial domain, and ask whether the temperature remains below a critical value in selected regions of the combustion domain. Our results show that in this example the kernel-based and the generalized Sobol' indices give qualitatively similar input importance rankings. Moreover, the ranking depends on the chosen observation window and can flip between different windows. The algorithms for implementing the proposed methods are provided in the supplementary materials and in an open source code repository.
tldr: The paper develops finite-element-based estimators for kernel-based (HSIC) and generalized Sobol' sensitivity indices of spatial sets, applied to a hydrogen combustion model.
motivation: Sensitivity analysis of spatially distributed outputs that exceed a threshold is computationally expensive because volume integrals over the spatial domain typically require Monte Carlo sampling.
method: Kernel-based sensitivity indices using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and function-valued generalized Sobol' indices are estimated by approximating spatial volume integrals with finite-element quadrature, avoiding Monte Carlo sampling over the domain.
result: For a 2D hydrogen combustion model governed by coupled convection-diffusion-reaction equations, kernel-based and generalized Sobol' indices give qualitatively similar input importance rankings, but the ranking depends on the chosen observation window and can flip between windows.
conclusion: The proposed finite-element quadrature approach makes kernel-based sensitivity analysis practical for expensive numerical models, while highlighting that conclusions about input importance are sensitive to the observation window selected.

title: PDE-constrained Inverse Problems At The $\sqrt{n}$ Rate Via Debiased Physics-informed Neural Networks
authors: Debarghya Mukherjee Yves Atchade
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of estimating unknown parameters in PDE-constrained inverse problems from noisy observations, where the PDE solution is approximated using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). While PINNs have demonstrated remarkable empirical success, existing estimators often inherit the slow nonparametric convergence rate of the neural-network solution, leading to biased and statistically inefficient inference for the finite-dimensional parameters of interest. To address this, we propose a two-step debiased estimation procedure that combines neural-network-based nonparametric estimation with an influence-function-based bias correction. By eliminating the first-order sensitivity of the estimator to errors in the nuisance function, our procedure yields a [MATH]-consistent and asymptotically normal estimator without requiring undersmoothing of the neural network component. We further extend this framework to Bayesian inference by replacing the original likelihood with a debiased quasi-likelihood and establish a Bernstein-von Mises theorem showing that the resulting posterior contracts at the [MATH]-rate with an asymptotic covariance matching that of the frequentist estimator. As a by-product of our analysis, we establish near-minimax optimal convergence rates for estimating a nonparametric regression function and its derivatives in Sobolev spaces using neural networks. Extensive numerical experiments corroborate our theoretical findings and demonstrate the necessity of the proposed debiasing procedure for valid statistical inference in PDE-constrained inverse problems.
tldr: The paper proposes a two-step debiased estimation procedure for PDE-constrained inverse problems solved with Physics-Informed Neural Networks, achieving √n-consistent and asymptotically normal estimators along with a Bernstein-von Mises theorem for the debiased quasi-posterior.
motivation: PINN-based estimators of finite-dimensional PDE parameters inherit the slow nonparametric convergence rate of the neural network solution, producing biased and statistically inefficient inference.
method: The authors combine neural-network-based nonparametric estimation with an influence-function-based bias correction, removing first-order sensitivity to nuisance-function error without undersmoothing, and extend the framework to Bayesian inference via a debiased quasi-likelihood.
result: They obtain √n-consistent asymptotically normal estimators and a Bernstein-von Mises theorem showing posterior contraction at the √n rate with matching asymptotic covariance, plus near-minimax convergence rates for neural-network estimation of Sobolev regression functions and derivatives.
conclusion: Debiasing is necessary and sufficient for valid statistical inference in PINN-based PDE-constrained inverse problems, as confirmed by numerical experiments.

title: Strongly Small-2 Sets Which Are Not Riesz Sets
authors: Przemys{\l}aw Ohrysko
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct spectral sets in discrete abelian groups which are strongly small-2 but are not Riesz sets. More precisely, on each of the compact groups [ (\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z)^{\mathbb N} \qquad\qquad (\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\mathbb N}, ] where (p) is an odd prime, there is a proper spectral set (E) such that [ |\alpha|*|\beta| \ll m ] for every (\alpha,\beta\in M_E(G)), although (M_E(G)) contains a nonzero singular measure. The latter may be chosen with mass one, Fourier support exactly (E), and convolution square in (L^2(G)). The construction combines an elementary finite-intersection criterion with a summable perturbation of a singular positive product measure. In the first model, the same full spectral support admits an amplitude family with an exact (\ell^2) absolute-continuity/singularity dichotomy. It also yields an uncountable family of mutually singular measures and an isometric copy of [ \ell^1\bigl((0,1/2]\bigr) ] in the square-zero quotient (M_E(G)/L^1_E(G)).
tldr: The paper constructs spectral sets in discrete abelian groups that are strongly small-2 but not Riesz sets, using a finite-intersection criterion and singular measure perturbation.
motivation: The work addresses a structural question in harmonic analysis on compact abelian groups, connecting spectral sets, Riesz sets, and properties of measures with Fourier support.
method: It combines an elementary finite-intersection criterion with a summable perturbation of a singular positive product measure to build the desired examples on groups such as (Z/6Z)^N and (Z/pZ)^N.
result: The construction yields proper spectral sets that are strongly small-2 but not Riesz, with a nonzero singular measure of mass one, exact Fourier support, and convolution square in L^2(G), plus additional families and an isometric copy of ℓ^1((0,1/2]) in a quotient.
conclusion: The paper provides new counterexamples in abstract harmonic analysis, separating the notions of strongly small-2 sets and Riesz sets in a broad class of compact abelian groups.

title: ChemMat-AgentSafetyBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Attacks And Defenses In Chemistry And Materials Agents
authors: Zhan'ao Yao, Zhihao Gao, Liang Yin, Boxuan Zhang, Xiaoyu Wu, Linjing Li, Rongyan Wang, Tingwei Chen, Youwei Wang, Xiaolin Zhao, Jiahui Shi, Jianjun Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chemistry and materials agents integrate literature retrieval, candidate generation, property prediction, and protocol planning into continuous discovery workflows. Consequently, the relevant safety question is shifting from whether a model answers a hazardous question to whether an agent releases a hazardous protocol through a tool-mediated workflow. We introduce \bench, a benchmark that evaluates whether chemistry and materials agents can be steered toward hazardous endpoints through user input, tool observations, or persistent memory. The benchmark contains 432 fixed harmful case specifications spanning eight hazard classes, three scenario shells, four tool-and-memory environments, a single-turn direct-attack baseline, and five online long-horizon attacks: intent hijacking, tool chaining, objective drifting, task injection, and memory poisoning. The concrete language of each online attack is generated from the evolving trajectory at runtime and is therefore not counted in the static benchmark size. In the four-model main experiment with a fixed attacker, agents release complete hazardous synthesis or preparation procedures in 25.6\% of runs. Replacing the attacker model yields mean success rates from 18.4\% to 26.5\%, indicating that the risk is not an artifact of a single attacker. Input- and state-level defenses adapted from general-purpose agent safety, as well as candidate checks designed for chemistry and materials, reduce some failures but still leave complete-path release rates between 9.2\% and 22.5\%. Existing defenses therefore do not simultaneously cover multi-entry contamination, tool state, and the final artifact boundary. These results highlight a widening gap between the rapid development of scientific agents and the safety evaluation and defenses available to the chemistry and materials community.
tldr: ChemMat-AgentSafetyBench is a benchmark for evaluating whether chemistry and materials agents can be steered into releasing hazardous protocols through user input, tool observations, or persistent memory.
motivation: As chemistry and materials agents move from question answering to tool-mediated discovery workflows, safety concerns shift from hazardous answers to hazardous protocol release through long-horizon agentic behavior.
method: The benchmark contains 432 fixed harmful case specifications across eight hazard classes, three scenario shells, and four tool-and-memory environments, plus a direct-attack baseline and five online long-horizon attacks generated at runtime.
result: Agents released complete hazardous synthesis or preparation procedures in 25.6% of runs with a fixed attacker, and mean success rates across attacker models ranged from 18.4% to 26.5%; adapted defenses still left complete-path release rates between 9.2% and 22.5%.
