conclusion: Existing defenses do not simultaneously cover multi-entry contamination, tool state, and final artifact boundaries, revealing a widening gap between scientific agent capabilities and safety evaluation.

title: A First-Principles Evaluation Of Graph-Based Network Intrusion Detection Systems
authors: Wajih Ul Hassan Rui Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-based network intrusion detection systems (GIDS) report strong benchmark detection metrics, but those metrics establish little about deployability. We approach the problem from first principles: rather than inheriting the preprocessing, windowing, and thresholding conventions of each published system, we ask what a controlled comparison requires and impose it uniformly. The result is GIDS-Eval, an evaluation framework that decomposes a GIDS into six interchangeable stages and turns those conventions into explicit experimental variables, so reported performance can be attributed to individual stages instead of whole pipelines. We survey nine representative GIDS, reimplement five of them within GIDS-Eval, and evaluate them on four datasets under one matched protocol. We identify nine recurring evaluation gaps and quantify the impact of each: two crafted edges achieve full evasion against three of the eight detector-dataset pairs with anything to hide; the snapshot window alone accounts for a mean 38.3% relative swing in average precision (AP); aligning preprocessing across systems moves AP by up to 61.8 percentage points for a single detector; and none of the 18 detector-dataset pairs we replay can alert as events arrive. We introduce GIDS-Lite, an encoder-free control built in the same framework, which ranks first by AP on two of the four datasets at up to 575[MATH] lower runtime. Architectural complexity is therefore not a consistent driver of detection quality under our matched protocol on current benchmarks, but it does enlarge the runtime, calibration, and attack surfaces operators must defend.
tldr: GIDS-Eval is a first-principles evaluation framework that decomposes graph-based network intrusion detection systems into six interchangeable stages to expose how preprocessing, windowing, and thresholding conventions drive reported detection performance.
motivation: Published graph-based intrusion detection systems report strong benchmark metrics, but those numbers reveal little about real-world deployability because each system inherits its own unstated preprocessing, windowing, and thresholding conventions.
method: The authors build GIDS-Eval, a modular evaluation framework with six interchangeable stages, survey nine representative GIDS, reimplement five of them, and evaluate all under one matched protocol across four datasets; they also introduce GIDS-Lite, an encoder-free control baseline.
result: Nine recurring evaluation gaps are identified and quantified: two crafted edges fully evade three of eight detector-dataset pairs, the snapshot window alone causes a mean 38.3% relative swing in average precision, aligning preprocessing shifts AP by up to 61.8 points, and no detector-dataset pair can alert as events arrive; GIDS-Lite ranks first by AP on two datasets at up to 575x lower runtime.
conclusion: Architectural complexity is not a consistent driver of detection quality under a matched protocol, but it enlarges runtime, calibration, and attack surfaces, so controlled evaluation is essential for deployment claims.

title: Subgroup Packing For Batched Pasta Transciphering
authors: Mugurel Barcau, Vicen\c{t}iu Pa\c{s}ol, George C. \c{t}urca\c{s}
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With transciphering, a server converts symmetrically encrypted records into homomorphic ciphertexts without learning the records or the symmetric key. For the PASTA cipher, this conversion involves dense linear maps whose implementation depends on how record words are arranged in the ciphertext. We ask whether rearranging a fixed batch can reduce its conversion cost. Instead of storing each record's words in a contiguous block, our layout interleaves records so that cyclic word shifts preserve each record's positions, which form a coset of a cyclic subgroup. For direct evaluation as a sum of masked translations, we characterize the required displacements and relate their counts, 255 for the contiguous layout and 128 for the subgroup layout, to a prior transversal-difference invariant. We implement three equally batched schedules for complete PASTA-3 conversion and subsequent public subset-sum queries in HElib. Across twelve paired corpora under six homomorphic keys, all 24 direct and subgroup conversions and all 48 subsequent queries return the expected values and required zeroes. The median paired ratio of direct to subgroup server cost is 1.60, including fresh public generation, conversion and two queries. The reduction comes with less remaining noise capacity. These results establish a packing-dependent cost--noise tradeoff.
tldr: The paper proposes a subgroup-based packing layout for batched PASTA transciphering that trades reduced homomorphic conversion cost for lower remaining noise capacity.
motivation: Transciphering converts symmetrically encrypted records into homomorphic ciphertexts, and the cost of PASTA conversion depends on how record words are arranged in ciphertexts.
method: They interleave records so cyclic word shifts preserve each record's coset structure, characterize required displacements, and implement three equally batched schedules for PASTA-3 conversion and subset-sum queries in HElib.
result: Across twelve paired corpora under six homomorphic keys, all conversions and queries succeed, with a median paired ratio of direct to subgroup server cost of 1.60, though the subgroup layout leaves less remaining noise capacity.
conclusion: The work establishes a packing-dependent cost-noise tradeoff for batched PASTA transciphering, improving server cost at the expense of noise budget.

title: Batten The Hatches: Cybersecurity With Military Mariners
authors: Ryan von Brock, Anna Raymaker, Animesh Chhotaray, Frank Li, Saman Zonouz, Raheem Beyah
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyberwarfare has become a key component of contemporary geopolitical conflict. However, there has been extremely limited systematic investigation into how cybersecurity is handled by military organizations and personnel. The military context is unique compared to other operational ones, with immense resource availability (U.S. military spending approached 1 trillion dollars in 2024), a rigid chain of command, and extraordinary consequences for its actions. Thus, military cybersecurity is a distinct yet understudied topic. In this paper, we take an early step at understanding military cybersecurity by investigating how service members understand, recognize, and respond to cyber risk. We focus on maritime services and carefully consider organizational barriers to design an unclassified study and conduct semi-structured interviews with 20 military mariners from U.S. Navy and Coast Guard vessels. Through our investigation, we identify unique consequences of compromising military systems, including weapon takeover and purposeful geopolitical escalation. We find that cybersecurity is organizationally abstract on ships, so mariners build cyber risk models from informal experience rather than formal instruction. They nonetheless make cybersecurity actionable by recognizing operational impacts and responding with a safety-oriented incident-response model that creates resilience but may delay cyber attribution and containment. These findings inform actionable recommendations to help military operators frame cyber threats, merge longstanding nautical doctrine with modern systems, and apply military insights to the civilian sector, all to secure the broader maritime environment.
tldr: A qualitative interview study of 20 U.S. Navy and Coast Guard mariners examining how military personnel understand and respond to cybersecurity risk aboard vessels.
motivation: Cyberwarfare is increasingly central to geopolitical conflict, yet there has been little systematic study of how military organizations and personnel handle cybersecurity, especially in the unique operational context of maritime services.
method: The authors designed an unclassified study accounting for organizational barriers and conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 military mariners from U.S. Navy and Coast Guard vessels.
result: Mariners develop cyber risk models from informal experience rather than formal instruction, and respond using a safety-oriented incident-response model that builds resilience but may delay cyber attribution and containment.
conclusion: The findings yield recommendations for framing cyber threats in military operations, merging nautical doctrine with modern systems, and transferring insights to the civilian maritime sector.

title: A Graph-Based Approach For Mapping Kernel-Level Telemetry To Mitre Att&ck
authors: Matteo Lupinacci, Luigi Arena, Francesco Blefari, Angelo Furfaro
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mapping observed system behavior to standardized frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK is essential for threat-informed defense, but remains largely manual. Existing automated methods depend on Cyber Threat Intelligence reports, which offer only retrospective accounts of attacks. Low-level telemetry, i.e. kernel-level system calls, instead provides evidence of adversary behavior, yet its volume and complexity have limited its use for automated mapping. We present a methodology that collects kernel-level events via eBPF, correlates attacker commands into a provenance graph, and derives compact graph representations suitable for LLM-based reasoning. These representations are mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework using both pure LLM prompting and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in the ATT&CK knowledge base, producing ranked technique candidates along with supporting rationales. We implement this methodology as an end-to-end pipeline, named Trace2ATT&CK and evaluate it on 347 Linux Atomic Red Team tests using locally deployed open-weights LLMs. RAG consistently improves ATT&CK mapping performance over pure prompting, while provenance graph substantially outperforms raw telemetry. These results show that local inference over graph-based behavioral descriptions can make automated ATT&CK mapping from kernel-level telemetry operationally viable, without compromising data confidentiality.
tldr: Trace2ATT&CK is an end-to-end pipeline that uses eBPF kernel-level telemetry, provenance graphs, and locally deployed open-weight LLMs with RAG to automatically map observed system behavior to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
motivation: Mapping adversary behavior to standardized frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK is essential for threat-informed defense but remains largely manual, and reliance on retrospective Cyber Threat Intelligence reports limits automated approaches.
method: The authors collect kernel-level events via eBPF, correlate attacker commands into a provenance graph, derive compact graph representations, and map them to ATT&CK using both pure LLM prompting and RAG grounded in the ATT&CK knowledge base.
result: Evaluated on 347 Linux Atomic Red Team tests with locally deployed open-weight LLMs, RAG consistently improved mapping performance over pure prompting, and provenance graph representations substantially outperformed raw telemetry.
conclusion: Local inference over graph-based behavioral descriptions makes automated ATT&CK mapping from kernel-level telemetry operationally viable without compromising data confidentiality, but the work lies entirely in cybersecurity and LLM systems.

title: Physics Based Triple Debye Dielectric Modeling And Multi Layer Ade Fdtd Simulation Of Terahertz Pulse Reflection For Breast Cancer Detection
authors: Mehran Shahmansouri Ali Asghar Molavi Choobini
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Terahertz (THz) imaging has emerged as a promising non-ionizing modality for breast cancer assessment owing to its intrinsic sensitivity to tissue hydration. However, existing dielectric descriptions of biological tissue, largely restricted to single- or double-Debye models, fail to capture the multiscale relaxation dynamics governing broadband THz dispersion and absorption, thereby limiting the quantitative interpretation of reflected pulse signatures.Here, a physics based triple Debye dielectric framework is developed to quantitatively predict broadband THz-tissue interactions. The proposed model explicitly incorporates three physically distinct relaxation processes associated with free-water rotational dynamics, bound-water relaxation ({\tau}_2), and ultrafast interfacial/macromolecular polarization ({\tau}_3). Model parameters are obtained by nonlinear least-squares fitting to experimentally measured refractive-index data digitized from published THz time-domain spectroscopy measurements of ex vivo human breast tissue. Compared with conventional Debye formulations, the proposed model substantially improves the fitting accuracy, reducing the root-mean-square error from 0.7773 (single Debye) and 0.2976 (double Debye) to only 0.0199 for the triple-Debye model. Fullwave FDTD ADE simulations of realistic multilayer breast structures further demonstrate that reflected THz pulses encode tissue hydration through reproducible temporal signatures, including increased reflection amplitude, delayed pulse arrival, and enhanced waveform broadening in malignant tissue. Polarization and angle resolved Fresnel analysis further indicates that hydration-dependent pseudo-Brewster minima provide an additional contrast mechanism by selectively suppressing reflections from low hydration normal and adipose tissues.
tldr: The paper develops a triple-Debye dielectric model and FDTD-ADE simulations of THz pulse reflection in multilayer breast tissue for breast cancer detection.
motivation: Existing single- and double-Debye models fail to capture multiscale relaxation dynamics underlying broadband THz dispersion and absorption in biological tissue, limiting quantitative interpretation of reflected pulse signatures.
method: A physics-based triple-Debye dielectric framework is parameterized using nonlinear least-squares fitting to published THz time-domain spectroscopy data of ex vivo human breast tissue, followed by full-wave FDTD ADE simulations of realistic multilayer breast structures and Fresnel polarization/angle-resolved analysis.
result: The triple-Debye model reduces fitting RMSE from 0.7773 and 0.2976 for single- and double-Debye models to 0.0199, and simulations show malignant tissue produces increased reflection amplitude, delayed pulse arrival, enhanced waveform broadening, and hydration-dependent pseudo-Brewster minima.
conclusion: The proposed model improves THz tissue characterization and suggests temporal and polarization-resolved reflection signatures as contrast mechanisms for breast cancer detection.

title: Towards Sustainable Hydrogen Systems: Supply Chain Optimization With Model Predictive Control And Reinforcement Learning
authors: Mahammad Valiyev
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hydrogen supply chains are expected to play a central role in future low-carbon energy systems by enabling renewable energy integration, long-duration storage, and decarbonization of industrial and transportation sectors. However, their operation is challenged by renewable generation variability, electricity price fluctuations, uncertain hydrogen demand, and engineering constraints associated with electrolyzers, energy storage, and grid interaction. As hydrogen infrastructure expands toward commercial deployment, operational strategies must balance economic performance, reliability, and sustainability under dynamic and uncertain conditions. This paper investigates and compares four control approaches for a renewable-powered hydrogen supply chain: a rule-based controller (RBC), model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning without forecasts (RL-NF), and reinforcement learning with forecast-augmented observations (RL-F). All methods are evaluated within a unified, physically realistic framework incorporating electrolyzer minimum-load and ramp-rate constraints, battery and hydrogen storage dynamics, grid import limits, and consistent economic assumptions, enabling a fair comparison under identical operating conditions. Simulation results show that MPC achieves the highest economic performance by exploiting short-term forecasts to coordinate storage, reduce grid dependence, and improve efficiency. RL-NF demonstrates robust and competitive performance without future information, highlighting the capability of learning-based methods to discover effective policies from experience. RL-F does not consistently outperform its no-forecast counterpart, suggesting that forecast uncertainty and increased state complexity can limit forecast-augmented learning. The results provide guidance for selecting operational control strategies in future hydrogen energy systems.
tldr: This paper compares rule-based control, model predictive control, and reinforcement learning strategies for operating a renewable-powered hydrogen supply chain under uncertainty.
motivation: Hydrogen supply chains are expected to be central to future low-carbon energy systems, but their operation is complicated by renewable variability, electricity price fluctuations, uncertain demand, and engineering constraints on electrolyzers and storage.
method: Four control approaches — rule-based control, MPC, RL without forecasts, and RL with forecast-augmented observations — are evaluated in a unified, physically realistic simulation framework with electrolyzer load/ramp constraints, battery and hydrogen storage dynamics, and grid import limits.
result: MPC achieves the best economic performance by exploiting short-term forecasts; RL-NF is robust and competitive without future information, while RL-F does not consistently outperform RL-NF due to forecast uncertainty and increased state complexity.
conclusion: The study offers guidance on selecting operational control strategies for future hydrogen energy systems, balancing economic performance, reliability, and sustainability.

title: Lyapunov Functions And $R$-Linear Convergence For Quadratic Barzilai-Borwein Dynamics
authors: Ya-Xiang Yuan Shutai Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Barzilai--Borwein (BB) method is [MATH]-linearly convergent on strongly convex quadratics, although neither the objective value nor the gradient norm is generally monotone. We construct an explicit current-point Lyapunov function for the quadratic dynamics after the warm-up step, assuming that both endpoints of the initial active spectrum survive this step. If [MATH] are these endpoints and [MATH] are the corresponding spectral projectors, then \[ (x) :=\lVert P_a\nabla f(x)\rVert^{{a+b}} \lVert P_b\nabla f(x)\rVert^{{a+b}} \] satisfies, for BB1, BB2, and every fixed positive weighted delayed Rayleigh rule, \[ (x_{k+1}) =\left({b+a}\right)^2 e^{-2D_{a,b}(\tau_k)}(x_k), \qquad D_{a,b}(\tau_k)\ge0, \] where [MATH] is the reciprocal step. The function is obtained by denormalizing the endpoint coboundary certificate in the sharp-rate analysis of Yang and Yuan. We prove that the endpoint exponents are the unique minimax choice among endpoint monomials and illustrate the Lyapunov law on a nonmonotone BB1 trajectory. Using this law, we also give a proof of [MATH]-linear convergence of the method in finite dimensions.
tldr: The paper constructs an explicit current-point Lyapunov function that certifies R-linear convergence of the Barzilai-Borwein method on strongly convex quadratic objectives.
motivation: The BB method converges R-linearly on strongly convex quadratics but neither the objective value nor gradient norm is monotone, so a non-standard Lyapunov certificate is needed to explain its convergence.
method: The authors denormalize an endpoint coboundary certificate from the sharp-rate analysis of Yang and Yuan to build a Lyapunov function based on spectral projectors of the surviving active spectrum, and prove the endpoint exponents are the unique minimax choice among endpoint monomials.
result: For BB1, BB2, and fixed positive weighted delayed Rayleigh rules, the Lyapunov function contracts multiplicatively with an explicit exponential decay rate depending on the reciprocal step, yielding a proof of R-linear convergence in finite dimensions.
conclusion: The construction clarifies the nonmonotone behavior of BB dynamics on quadratics, provides a rigorous R-linear convergence proof, and is illustrated on a nonmonotone BB1 trajectory.

title: $R$-Linear Convergence Of Barzilai-Borwein Methods On Strictly Convex Quadratics Via Closed-Cone Homogeneous Dynamics
authors: Ya-Xiang Yuan Shutai Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an [MATH]-linear convergence proof for BB1, BB2, and fixed positive spectral-weight variants on finite-dimensional strictly convex quadratics. The delayed recurrence is written as a first-order system on the closed cone of compatible consecutive-gradient pairs. Its transition is continuous and positively homogeneous of degree one, including at finite termination. A compactness theorem shows that pointwise convergence of every cone orbit implies a uniform finite-step contraction and hence a global [MATH]-linear estimate. By a realization lemma, every compatible state initiates a BB1 trajectory, so Raydan's theorem yields pointwise stability on the entire cone. Finally, the transformation [MATH] conjugates every fixed positive spectral-weight rule to BB1. Consequently, BB1, BB2, and all such weighted rules have the same homogeneous growth radius.
tldr: The paper proves R-linear convergence for Barzilai-Borwein methods on strictly convex quadratic functions using a closed-cone homogeneous dynamical systems approach.
motivation: Barzilai-Borwein methods are popular gradient methods, but their convergence properties on quadratics are not fully understood, especially for spectral-weight variants.
method: The authors model consecutive-gradient pairs as states on a closed cone and study a positively homogeneous first-order transition map, using compactness and a realization lemma to transfer pointwise stability to uniform finite-step contraction.
result: They establish global R-linear convergence for BB1, BB2, and all fixed positive spectral-weight variants, and show these rules share the same homogeneous growth radius.
conclusion: The closed-cone dynamical framework provides a unified convergence analysis for Barzilai-Borwein type methods on strictly convex quadratics.

title: Global And Unconditional $R$-Linear Convergence Of Rank-Compressed Weighted Lmsd Sweeps For Strictly Convex Quadratics
authors: Ya-Xiang Yuan Shutai Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study limited memory steepest descent (LMSD) with exact algebraic rank compression for strictly convex quadratic optimization. At each cycle, the method restricts the gradient history to its column space and applies the reciprocals of all Ritz values of the compressed projection in the next sweep. If the block-start gradient has at most [MATH] active distinct eigenvalues, the delayed sweep terminates finitely. For nonterminating trajectories, a determinant and Cauchy--Binet formula for the complete-sweep polynomial yields global convergence without a full-rank history or a run-wise normalized-conditioning bound. Consecutive sweep endpoints define a continuous positively homogeneous map on a closed cone of compatible states. Compactness then gives an [MATH]-linear endpoint estimate, uniform over compatible initial states, with constants depending only on [MATH] and [MATH]; the estimate extends to inner gradients, iterate errors, and objective gaps. Every fixed positive spectral weight [MATH] is linearly conjugate to the standard method. The weighted methods therefore share its decay factor, while the Euclidean-norm prefactor is increased by at most [MATH]. This includes harmonic-Ritz LMSD, fixed power weights, and the delayed BB1 and BB2 recurrences.
tldr: The paper analyzes global convergence and R-linear convergence rates of rank-compressed weighted limited memory steepest descent (LMSD) sweeps for strictly convex quadratic optimization.
motivation: Limited memory steep descent methods are important for large-scale optimization, and understanding their convergence properties under rank compression and spectral weighting remains an open problem.
method: The authors use exact algebraic rank compression of gradient history, apply reciprocals of Ritz values in each sweep, and derive determinant and Cauchy-Binet formulas for the complete-sweep polynomial to establish convergence.
result: They prove finite termination under an active eigenvalue condition, global convergence for nonterminating trajectories, and an R-linear endpoint estimate uniform over compatible initial states, with constants depending only on problem parameters.
conclusion: Weighted LMSD variants, including harmonic-Ritz and BB1/BB2 recurrences, share the same decay factor as the standard method, with only a modest increase in the Euclidean-norm prefactor.

title: Random Access And Localization In Cell-Free User-Centric Networks With Multipath Channels
authors: Simon Tarboush, Eleni Gkiouzepi, Giuseppe Caire
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a wireless network, the initial/random access mechanism (RACH) allows idle/new users to join the network and (possibly) request allocated transmission resources for subsequent traffic. Building on our own previous work, for cell-free user-centric networks, we consider location-dependent random access codebooks such that users in a certain geographic area (location) make use of the corresponding set of random access preambles (codewords). We expand our previous work in two ways: (1) we consider multipath channels with line-of-sight (LoS) propagation within a given radius; (2) we consider two different approaches. The first makes use of Zadoff-Chu (ZC) sequences and GLRT detection to cope with the unknown delay, and it is conceptually similar to the 3GPP 2-step RACH specification (here extended to the cell-free case). The second builds on our previous work on multisource approximate message passing (AMP). For both schemes, we also consider a novel near Maximum-Likelihood approach for localization of the random access users directly from the detected RACH preambles, implicitly using angle of arrival and time difference of arrival information embedded into the LoS components. Simulation results show that the AMP approach achieves generally better performance for random access user detection, while both approaches have similar localization capability with a slight superiority for the frequency-domain scheme.
tldr: The paper develops location-dependent random access and localization schemes for cell-free user-centric wireless networks with multipath channels, using Zadoff-Chu sequences with GLRT and multisource approximate message passing (AMP).
motivation: Initial random access is essential for idle/new users to join wireless networks, and cell-free user-centric architectures require location-aware preamble allocation to handle multipath propagation and enable user localization.
method: The authors extend prior work by considering multipath channels with line-of-sight propagation, and propose two approaches: one based on Zadoff-Chu sequences with GLRT detection similar to 3GPP 2-step RACH, and another based on multisource approximate message passing; both include near-ML localization using angle-of-arrival and time-difference-of-arrival information.
result: Simulations show the AMP approach generally achieves better random access user detection performance, while both schemes have similar localization capability with a slight advantage for the frequency-domain scheme.
conclusion: The proposed location-dependent random access and localization schemes are viable for cell-free user-centric networks with multipath channels, with AMP offering better detection and frequency-domain processing slightly improving localization.

title: Internal Controllability Of First Order Quasilinear Hyperbolic Systems With A Reduced Number Of Controls
authors: Fatiha Alabau-Boussouira, Jean-Michel Coron, Guillaume Olive
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we investigate the exact controllability of [MATH] first order one-dimensional quasilinear hyperbolic systems by [MATH] internal controls that are localized in space in some part of the domain. We distinguish two situations. The first one is when the equations of the system have the same speed. In this case, we can use the method of characteristics and obtain a simple and complete characterization for linear systems. Thanks to a linear test this also provides some sufficient conditions for the local exact controllability around the trajectories of semilinear systems. However, when the speed of the equations are not anymore the same, we see that we encounter the problem of loss of derivatives if we try to control quasilinear systems with a reduced number of controls. To solve this problem, as in a prior article by J.-M. Coron and P. Lissy on a Navier-Stokes control system, we first use the notion of algebraic solvability due to M. Gromov. However, in contrast with this prior article where a standard fixed point argument could be used to treat the nonlinearities, we use here a fixed point theorem of Nash-Moser type due to M. Gromov in order to handle the problem of loss of derivatives.
tldr: The paper studies internal exact controllability of first-order one-dimensional quasilinear hyperbolic systems using a reduced number of localized controls.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize exact controllability for quasilinear hyperbolic systems when controls are localized and fewer than the number of equations, addressing the loss of derivatives that arises when speeds differ.
method: They use the method of characteristics for equal speeds, a linear test for semilinear local controllability, and Gromov's algebraic solvability plus a Nash-Moser fixed-point theorem to handle loss of derivatives in the quasilinear case with different speeds.
result: For equal speeds, they obtain a simple and complete characterization for linear systems and sufficient conditions for local exact controllability of semilinear systems; for different speeds, they overcome loss of derivatives via the Nash-Moser approach.
conclusion: The work provides controllability conditions for quasilinear hyperbolic systems with reduced localized controls, extending techniques from algebraic solvability and Nash-Moser theory to this PDE control setting.

title: Normal Equations And Discrete Energy Structures For High-Order Streamline Diffusion
authors: Erik Burman, Peter Hansbo, Mats G. Larson
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyse fully discrete Streamline Diffusion finite element methods, also known as SUPG methods, for time-dependent first-order systems with skew-symmetric spatial operators. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first stability and a priori error analysis of strongly consistent Streamline Diffusion finite elements combined with linear multistep schemes of order greater than two for multidimensional first-order hyperbolic systems. Local-in-time [MATH]-residual minimisation singles out [MATH], where [MATH] is the stabilisation parameter, [MATH] the time step, and [MATH] the current-time coefficient in the method average. For this choice, each implicit linear system is a symmetric positive definite normal equation in a graph norm. A direct dual-residual estimate yields errors of order [MATH] when [MATH] is proportional to [MATH] and [MATH], where [MATH] is the mesh size, [MATH] the polynomial degree, and [MATH] the temporal order. Stability is established for the [MATH]-method and the Adams-Moulton methods AM3-AM5. The general-degree AM3 and AM4 estimates use strengthened CFL conditions; for continuous piecewise affine elements, an elementwise cancellation recovers the standard hyperbolic regime. AM5 and the explicit Adams-Bashforth methods AB3 and AB4 are stable under a standard hyperbolic CFL condition, though the explicit schemes do not have normal-equation structure. Order-matched acoustic tests recover orders two through five and material-residual rates one half-order lower. In a d'Alembert test with discontinuous initial data, normal-equation SUPG recovers second-order local [MATH] convergence away from the wave fronts, whereas the unstabilised error is close to half order. A two-dimensional compact-wave test shows improved localisation with modest dissipation.
tldr: This paper develops stability and a priori error analysis for fully discrete Streamline Diffusion (SUPG) finite element methods coupled with high-order linear multistep time integrators for multidimensional first-order hyperbolic systems.
motivation: High-order time stepping combined with strongly consistent streamline diffusion stabilisation for first-order hyperbolic systems lacked a rigorous stability and error analysis, particularly for multistep schemes of order greater than two.
method: The authors analyse SUPG finite elements with local-in-time residual minimisation that selects a specific stabilisation parameter, yielding implicit linear systems that are symmetric positive definite normal equations in a graph norm; they prove dual-residual error estimates and establish stability for the theta-method and Adams-Moulton/Adams-Bashforth schemes.
result: Errors of optimal order are obtained when the stabilisation parameter scales appropriately with mesh size, polynomial degree, and temporal order; numerical acoustic, d'Alembert, and compact-wave tests confirm orders two through five and improved localisation of sharp features.
conclusion: The normal-equation SUPG framework provides a provably stable and accurate high-order discretisation for first-order hyperbolic systems, recovering near-optimal local convergence even with discontinuous initial data.

title: A Parameterized Block Lu Preconditioning For Double Saddle Point Problems
authors: Hamed Aslani, Mehdi Najafi Kalyani, Davod Khojasteh Salkuyeh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a biparametric preconditioning technique for large, sparse, non-symmetric, and non-singular double saddle point problems. The preconditioner is induced using a stationary iteration method. It is also based on a two-parameterized block LU factorization of the coefficient matrix. To begin with, some convergence results of the iteration method are derived. Moreover, the spectral features exhibited by the preconditioned matrix are given. Finally, the presented preconditioner is conjuncted with the GMRES method. Numerical results demonstrate the satisfactory performance of the preconditioner.
tldr: The paper proposes a biparametric block LU preconditioner for double saddle point problems and evaluates it with GMRES.
motivation: Large sparse nonsymmetric double saddle point systems arise in various applications and require efficient iterative solvers.
method: A stationary iteration and two-parameterized block LU factorization are used to construct a preconditioner; convergence and spectral properties are analyzed.
result: Numerical experiments show satisfactory performance when the preconditioner is combined with GMRES.
conclusion: The proposed parameterized block LU preconditioning is effective for double saddle point problems, though it lies outside quantum information research.

title: IDORacle: Template-Guided SQL-Sink Mediation For Object-Level Authorization In Java Applications
authors: Yuewantong Song, Guanhang Shi, Yin Cai, Changhui Wang, Jin Wei, Ping Chen, Lei Shi, Jiangxing Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR), often modeled as Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA), remains prevalent in Java database applications because identity and authorization checks at the controller or service layer are disconnected from SQL execution based on resource identifiers. Existing work largely detects these vulnerabilities but offers limited low-intrusion runtime protection for legacy Java-SQL applications. We present IDORacle, a template-guided SQL-sink interception and rewriting framework for preventing horizontal privilege escalation at runtime. IDORacle propagates authenticated identity context across HTTP requests, asynchronous tasks, and data-access boundaries through a server-side trace identifier. At the MyBatis/JDBC boundary, it extracts SQL templates, computes dual fingerprints, and performs one-time template analysis to generate reusable mediation plans. During execution, it combines subject context, SQL ASTs, table metadata, and cached authorization proofs to permit, rewrite, or block operations. Its guard model supports direct ownership predicates, join-derived ownership, probes for group-owned resources, role-sensitive state transitions, and sensitive-column mediation. A Java-SQL benchmark grounded in real-world CVE reports shows that IDORacle prevents the tested horizontal authorization violations with a worst-case guard latency of 0.17 ms. Redundancy-aware optimization reduces average per-instance overhead by more than 90%, to 0.017 ms for hot SQL templates.
tldr: IDORacle is a runtime SQL-sink interception framework that prevents insecure direct object reference (IDOR/BOLA) vulnerabilities in Java applications by mediating authorization at the database query boundary.
motivation: IDOR/BOLA remains a common vulnerability in Java database applications because controller/service-layer authorization checks are disconnected from SQL execution based on resource identifiers, and existing tools offer limited low-intrusion runtime protection.
method: IDORacle propagates authenticated identity context across requests and asynchronous tasks using a server-side trace identifier, extracts SQL templates and dual fingerprints at the MyBatis/JDBC boundary, generates reusable mediation plans, and permits, rewrites, or blocks SQL operations using subject context, ASTs, metadata, and cached proofs.
result: On a Java-SQL benchmark based on real CVEs, IDORacle prevented tested horizontal authorization violations with worst-case guard latency of 0.17 ms, and redundancy-aware optimization reduced average overhead by over 90%, to 0.017 ms for hot SQL templates.
conclusion: Template-guided SQL-sink mediation offers an effective and low-overhead runtime defense against IDOR/BOLA in legacy Java applications, though it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Omniscience For The Masses: New Threats In The Metaverse's Democratized World Creation
authors: Andrea Mengascini, Ryan Aurelio, Jason Polakis, Giancarlo Pellegrino
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metaverse platforms increasingly derive their success from user-generated virtual worlds: self-contained social and interactive environments, which can be created by any ordinary user and scale to billions of visits. Platforms such as Roblox, Horizon Worlds, and VRChat now host millions of creator-built worlds that govern how users see, hear, and interact with one another. While this model enables rapid growth and creativity, it fundamentally delegates control over social interactions and world behavior to untrusted users. In this paper, we present the first systematic security and privacy assessment of metaverse world creators. We survey 25 platforms that support user-created worlds and analyze their world-creation capabilities. Guided by this analysis, we design and implement five novel attacks that exploit creator-provided tools to violate spatial, visual, and auditory constraints in immersive environments, enabling covert user surveillance and manipulation without software vulnerabilities or developer-level privileges. We further show that five previously-proposed attacks can be replicated using only standard world-creation features. Finally, we find that existing platform vetting, runtime protections, and creator policies are insufficient to mitigate malicious world-creator behavior, revealing a fundamental mismatch between users' privacy expectations and the powers granted to world creators.
tldr: The paper presents the first systematic security and privacy assessment of metaverse world creators, revealing novel attacks that exploit standard world-creation tools.
motivation: Metaverse platforms increasingly rely on user-generated virtual worlds, delegating control over social interactions to untrusted creators, which raises unexamined security and privacy risks.
method: The authors survey 25 platforms supporting user-created worlds, analyze their creation capabilities, and design five novel attacks that violate spatial, visual, and auditory constraints, while also replicating five previously proposed attacks.
result: The attacks enable covert user surveillance and manipulation without software vulnerabilities or developer privileges, and existing platform vetting and runtime protections fail to mitigate malicious creator behavior.
conclusion: There is a fundamental mismatch between users' privacy expectations and the powers granted to world creators, highlighting the need for better protections in democratized metaverse environments.

title: MicroHasTEE: Bare-Metal Haskell For Type-Level Peripheral Ownership On Armv8-M
authors: Robert Krook
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Arm TrustZone for Armv8-M isolates Secure and Non-secure software, but developers must still coordinate peripheral attribution, interrupt routing, initialization, and gateway interfaces across separately built firmware images. Inconsistent assumptions between these images can compile successfully and emerge only as faults on the target device. We present MicroHasTEE, a multiparty programming framework that expresses both firmware applications as participants in one typed Haskell program. MicroHasTEE represents peripheral authority with type-level capability ledgers and uses indexed setup computations to track resource acquisition, configuration, transfer, and finalization. Domain-specific effect types restrict peripheral operations and interrupt callbacks to the participant that holds the corresponding authority, while typed callable handles describe the Secure services available to Non-secure code. MicroHs compiles the shared program twice to produce separate bare-metal Secure and Non-secure firmware images. We implement MicroHasTEE for an STM32U5 Nucleo board, including TrustZone configuration, peripheral drivers, and a serialized gateway for cross-domain Haskell calls. For programs expressed through its interface, MicroHasTEE rejects inconsistent resource use, attribution changes after configuration, callbacks in the wrong domain, and calls to unregistered Secure services. A door-lock case study demonstrates feasibility, with firmware images occupying 232.7 KiB and 228.4 KiB of flash and approximately 220 KiB of SRAM per domain.
tldr: MicroHasTEE is a multiparty programming framework that encodes Arm TrustZone Secure/Non-secure peripheral ownership and interrupt routing as type-level capabilities in a shared bare-metal Haskell program compiled into two separate firmware images.
motivation: Armv8-M TrustZone isolates Secure and Non-secure software, but developers must manually coordinate peripheral attribution, initialization, and gateway interfaces across separately built firmware images, where inconsistent assumptions compile cleanly yet fail only on hardware.
method: The framework represents peripheral authority using type-level capability ledgers and indexed setup computations that track resource acquisition, configuration, transfer, and finalization, with domain-specific effect types restricting peripheral operations and interrupt callbacks to the owning participant; MicroHs compiles the shared program twice to produce bare-metal Secure and Non-secure images.
result: Implemented on an STM32U5 Nucleo board with TrustZone configuration, peripheral drivers, and a serialized cross-domain gateway, MicroHasTEE statically rejects inconsistent resource use, post-configuration attribution changes, wrong-domain callbacks, and calls to unregistered Secure services, with a door-lock case study fitting in roughly 230 KiB flash and 220 KiB SRAM per domain.
conclusion: Type-level capability tracking in a multiparty Haskell DSL provides a practical, verifiable way to enforce TrustZone peripheral ownership and cross-domain interface consistency in embedded firmware development.

title: A Feature-Rich Embedded Nids With eBPF/XDP: Detector And Architecture Trade-offs
authors: Shiqi Wu, Oleksii Koshovyi, Georgios Pseiridis Pseiras, Victor Morel, Romaric Duvignau
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks remain a serious threat to transport networks, with recent attack volumes exceeding 30 Tbps, and the telecommunications industry being the main target. Recent work has yet to study the impact of the hosting software architecture on network monitoring solutions, or to assess recent algorithms for improving attack detection. This paper presents a Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) for DDoS detection in transport networks, developed in collaboration with Ericsson. Building on a statistical baseline, we improve detection effectiveness with an Isolation Forest trained on a wider set of flow features, extracted by GoFlowMeter, our open-source Go implementation of CICFlowMeter, and we integrate eBPF/XDP so that the NIDS filters real traffic at the kernel level. We further compare three deployments, monolithic, Kafka-based, and gRPC-based microservices, on a Raspberry Pi 5 testbed replaying the CIC-DDoS2019 dataset as real network traffic. Detection quality is governed mainly by the choice of detector rather than by the transport: the Isolation Forest raises recall and F1 score (0.965 live in the monolithic variant) over the baseline by flagging low-volume attack windows that the baseline misses. The transport is not neutral, however: gRPC reaches almost the same accuracy as the monolithic variant while adding less than 2 milliseconds of transport time per window, whereas the asynchronous Kafka pipeline trails by roughly nine percentage points and adds about 27 milliseconds. These findings clarify the trade-off between detection quality and architectural overhead when deploying a NIDS on resource-constrained hardware.
tldr: The paper presents a feature-rich embedded network intrusion detection system using eBPF/XDP and compares monolithic, Kafka-based, and gRPC-based microservice architectures for DDoS detection on a Raspberry Pi 5 testbed.
motivation: DDoS attacks remain a major threat to transport networks, and there is limited study of how hosting software architecture affects network monitoring and detection effectiveness.
method: The authors build on a statistical baseline, train an Isolation Forest on expanded flow features extracted by GoFlowMeter, integrate eBPF/XDP for kernel-level filtering, and compare three deployments (monolithic, Kafka-based, gRPC-based) on a Raspberry Pi 5 using the CIC-DDoS2019 dataset replayed as live traffic.
result: The Isolation Forest improves recall and F1 over the baseline (0.965 live F1 in the monolithic variant), with gRPC achieving near-monolithic accuracy while adding <2 ms transport time, whereas the Kafka pipeline trails by about nine percentage points and adds roughly 27 ms.
conclusion: Detection quality is governed mainly by the detector choice rather than the transport, but transport architecture introduces non-negligible overhead; the work clarifies trade-offs for deploying NIDS on resource-constrained hardware.

title: Evaluating Context Segmentation In Locally Deployable SLMs For Cybersecurity Ctf Tasks
authors: Michele Lotto Sebastiano Nordio
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The proliferation of highly capable open-weight Small Language Models (SLMs) democratizes access to advanced cybersecurity capabilities, posing a escalating risk as these models can bypass proprietary API guardrails when deployed locally. However, SLMs deployed as autonomous agents often struggle with long-horizon, exploratory tasks like cybersecurity Capture The Flag (CTF) challenges due to context bloat and cognitive degradation from accumulated tool-call outputs. To understand and mitigate this cybersecurity threat, we introduce , a two-level agentic framework that divides complex exploitation tasks into manageable, contextually isolated sub-problems. Evaluating on the dataset using memory-constrained models, we demonstrate that for the E4B model, our strategy acts as an intelligent search, achieving competitive rewards with superior token efficiency compared to brute-force retries, and successfully solving 18.52\% of tasks that standard agentic execution fails to complete. Code is available at [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes a two-level agentic framework that segments context for locally deployed small language models to improve performance on cybersecurity Capture The Flag tasks.
motivation: The increasing capability of open-weight small language models poses cybersecurity risks, but their performance on long-horizon exploratory tasks is hindered by context bloat and cognitive degradation.
method: The authors introduce a framework that decomposes complex exploitation tasks into contextually isolated sub-problems, evaluating it with memory-constrained models on a CTF dataset.
result: For the E4B model, the approach achieves competitive rewards with better token efficiency than brute-force retries and solves 18.52% of tasks that standard agentic execution fails to complete.
conclusion: Context segmentation can act as intelligent search, enabling small language models to tackle complex cybersecurity tasks more effectively despite memory constraints.

title: Forging Tree-Ring: Reproducing And Instrumenting Black-Box Semantic Watermark Forgery
authors: Saifur Rahman Tamim, Md Taslimul Hasan Toufique, A. M. Tayeful Islam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic watermarking schemes such as Tree-Ring hide a detectable pattern in the initial noise latent of a diffusion model. Recent work shows these watermarks are not only removable but forgeable: an attacker who never sees the watermarking key can still produce images the genuine detector accepts. We reproduce the Reprompt forgery attack of M\"uller et al. against Tree-Ring on Stable Diffusion XL, using the authors' released code, on free-tier dual T4 GPUs with 14.6 GB of usable memory per device, substantially less per-GPU memory than the A40 hardware used in the original study. The attack reproduces. Over six trials of three arms we detect genuine images 6/6, clean images 0/6, and forged images 5/6, at 325-332 s per attack. Three further results came out of running it under constraint. The released detector computes a non-central [MATH] statistic and hands back only its CDF, so we recovered the discarded statistic; our recovery matches the released detector exactly, and two natural scores built from it separate the forged arm from the clean null at AUC 0.861 and 0.972 on the same eighteen observations. Running SDXL in half precision requires patching the pipeline's direct autoencoder calls, and a controlled probe confirms the patched path leaves the detector statistic unchanged. Finally, we report a prediction we made from reading the detector source that our measurements then contradicted. The notebook, the pinned fork and every measurement artifact are released with the paper.
tldr: The paper reproduces and instruments a black-box forgery attack on the Tree-Ring semantic watermark for diffusion models under constrained GPU memory.
motivation: Semantic watermarks such as Tree-Ring are used to detect AI-generated images, but recent work claims they are forgeable by an attacker without the watermarking key. The authors aim to reproduce this claim and characterize the attack under limited hardware.
method: Using the released code for the Reprompt attack, they run six trials across three arms on Stable Diffusion XL with free-tier dual T4 GPUs, recover a discarded non-central statistic from the detector's CDF, and patch half-precision pipeline calls with a controlled probe.
result: Genuine images are detected 6/6, clean images 0/6, and forged images 5/6, with attack times of 325–332 s. The recovered statistic matches the released detector exactly, and two scores built from it separate forged from clean with AUC 0.861 and 0.972.
conclusion: The Reprompt forgery attack reproduces under reduced memory, and the instrumented analysis exposes additional discriminative information from the detector's discarded statistic while highlighting a failed prediction from source inspection.

title: Diverse Minds, Divided Networks? Personality Composition, Polarization, And Collective Intelligence In LLM-Based Social Simulations
authors: Raad Bin Tareaf
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulated societies of large language model agents are used to study online polarization, and separately to study collective intelligence, but the two are rarely measured in the same system. It is therefore difficult to say whether a society's personality composition shapes both, or whether reducing polarization costs collective competence. We present TraitMix, an experimental design in which the Big Five composition of a simulated social network, both trait levels and trait heterogeneity, is a controlled experimental variable, and in which polarization and collective performance are measured in the same runs. Across 991 simulations of hundred-agent societies, spanning six contested topics and six language models, trait heterogeneity has the largest measured effects, acting in opposite directions on two faces of polarization: varied societies hold more dispersed opinions while being less segregated into camps, so homogeneous societies are not moderate but consensual echo chambers. Trait effects are not additive, as Agreeableness determines the sign of Openness, an interaction that replicates across models although the primary model's estimate is influence-driven. Contrary to the trade-off the study was designed to measure, no polarization measure predicts poorer collective performance, and cross-cutting interaction is the only one of four whose association with collective accuracy survives partialling on the aggregation identity. We report ablations removing two potential measurement circularities, an induction gate applied to every model, and the measures that failed them.
tldr: TraitMix uses 991 simulations of hundred-agent LLM societies to test whether Big Five personality composition controls polarization and collective intelligence in the same system.
motivation: Simulated LLM societies study online polarization and collective intelligence separately, making it unclear whether personality composition shapes both or whether reducing polarization harms collective competence.
method: The Big Five composition (trait levels and heterogeneity) of a simulated social network is treated as a controlled experimental variable, with polarization and collective performance measured in identical runs across six contested topics and six language models, plus ablations and induction gates.
result: Trait heterogeneity has the largest effects, pushing opinion dispersion up but camp segregation down, so homogeneous societies form consensual echo chambers; Agreeableness flips the sign of Openness, and no polarization measure predicts worse collective performance.
conclusion: The hypothesized polarization–competence trade-off is not observed; only cross-cutting interaction predicts collective accuracy once aggregation identity is partialled out, reframing how personality composition shapes LLM-simulated societies.

title: Global Maps Of Travel Time To Emergency And Tertiary Hospitals
authors: Johan Emilsson
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Global estimates of access to health care treat every facility alike. Drive time was routed on the OpenStreetMap network from all 217,841 of its hospitals and 15-, 30- and 60-minute isochrones dissolved for nested capability tiers, weighted with GHS-POP 2025. 96.2% of the world's population lives within an hour's drive of a hospital, 78.5% of a hospital with a documented emergency department, and 40.3% of one with a helipad or university name marking tertiary care. The 1.45 billion people within an hour of a hospital but not of an emergency hospital live mainly in South and East Asia and Nigeria; the 312 million beyond an hour of any hospital lie in a belt from the Sahel to Madagascar. Defining the tertiary tier by helipad alone leaves its estimate unchanged, and the isochrone construction shifts the 60-minute figures by a few percent. Counting every facility as equivalent overstates access to time-critical care.
tldr: A geospatial analysis computing global drive-time isochrones to hospitals, distinguishing emergency and tertiary care tiers to produce more accurate health-care accessibility estimates.
motivation: Existing global estimates of health-care access treat all facilities as equivalent, ignoring differences in facility capability, which misrepresents access to time-critical emergency and tertiary care.
method: Drive times were routed on the OpenStreetMap road network from all 217,841 mapped hospitals, with 15-, 30- and 60-minute isochrones computed and dissolved for nested capability tiers, then population-weighted using GHS-POP 2025.
result: 96.2% of the world's population lives within an hour's drive of any hospital, but only 78.5% of an emergency hospital and 40.3% of a tertiary-care facility; 1.45 billion people have hospital but not emergency access, and 312 million are beyond an hour of any hospital.
conclusion: Treating all facilities as equivalent substantially overstates access to time-critical care, and defining tertiary care by helipad alone does not materially alter the estimates.

title: Solving Large-Scale Sparse Linear Complementarity Problems Using A Shifted-Splitting Multi-Parameter Modulus-Based Iteration Method
authors: Abhishek Kumar Singh Sengar, Bharat Kumar, Deepmala
abstract: ArXiv:2609.11949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A shifted-splitting multi-parameter modulus-based iteration method is proposed for solving large sparse linear complementarity problems. The method introduces two additional parameters through a shifted matrix splitting while preserving the original coefficient matrix. Suitable choices of the splitting matrices generate Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, SOR, and AOR-type schemes; the Gauss-Seidel type form is considered in the numerical experiments. Sufficient convergence results are established for [MATH]-matrices and [MATH]-matrices by using the spectral radius of the associated iteration matrix. For structured sparse matrices, sufficient parameter intervals ensuring the convergence of the proposed method are derived. An algorithm based on grid search is also developed to select efficient near-optimal parameter pairs for the numerical implementation. The influence of different parameter-matrix choices is examined through a sensitivity analysis. Numerical experiments on standard large sparse test problems demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed method compared with the tested projected-type method, the new modulus-based matrix splitting method, and the modulus-based matrix double splitting method in terms of iteration count, residual, and CPU time.
tldr: A shifted-splitting multi-parameter modulus-based iteration method is proposed for efficiently solving large sparse linear complementarity problems.
motivation: Large sparse linear complementarity problems arise in many applied settings, and existing modulus-based matrix splitting solvers can be slow or limited in their convergence behavior.
method: The authors introduce a shifted matrix splitting with two additional parameters, encompassing Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, SOR, and AOR-type schemes, and derive sufficient convergence conditions via the spectral radius of the iteration matrix for H- and L-matrices, along with a grid-search algorithm for near-optimal parameter selection.
result: Numerical experiments on standard large sparse test problems show the proposed method outperforms projected-type, new modulus-based matrix splitting, and modulus-based matrix double splitting methods in iteration count, residual, and CPU time.
conclusion: The shifted-splitting multi-parameter modulus-based approach offers an efficient and tunable solver for large sparse linear complementarity problems, with validated convergence guarantees and empirical speedups.

title: Wasserstein Spaces Have The Radon-Nikodym Property
authors: Charles Bertucci
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wasserstein spaces carry two natural geometries: a vertical one, inherited from the linear structure of signed measures, and a horizontal one, induced by couplings. We prove that a Radon-Nikodym property holds in both. In the vertical geometry, bounded subsets of [MATH] are dentable in an ambient Banach space which itself fails the Radon-Nikodym property; we derive variational principles, Radon-Nikodym theorems for vector measures and martingale convergence results. In the horizontal geometry, we show that a Radon-Nikodym property is inherited from the one of spaces of random variables. We introduce horizontal martingales and prove that they are exactly the laws of [MATH] -valued martingales.
tldr: The paper proves Radon-Nikodym-type properties for Wasserstein spaces under both their vertical (linear-structure) and horizontal (coupling-induced) geometries.
motivation: Wasserstein spaces carry two natural geometries, and the authors aim to understand which geometric/analytic properties (notably the Radon-Nikodym property) hold in each, connecting optimal transport to Banach space theory.
method: Functional-analytic techniques are used: dentability of bounded subsets in an ambient Banach space, variational principles, Radon-Nikodym theorems for vector measures, and martingale convergence arguments; the horizontal case is reduced to properties of spaces of random variables.
result: Bounded subsets of the vertical Wasserstein space are shown to be dentable even though the ambient Banach space fails the Radon-Nikodym property, and a horizontal Radon-Nikodym property is inherited from random-variable spaces, with horizontal martingales identified as laws of martingales.
conclusion: The findings establish that Wasserstein spaces possess Radon-Nikodym-type structure in both geometries, with implications for vector measures, variational principles, and martingale theory.

title: Transform Before Linearizing: Robust Newton Methods For Singular $p$-Laplace And $p$-Stokes Equations
authors: Gonzalo G. de Diego, Fortino Garcia, Georg Stadler, Kewei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For [MATH], the [MATH]-Laplace equation and its [MATH]-Stokes generalization are difficult to solve numerically. Newton's method converges rapidly only close to the solution, with iteration counts that grow under mesh refinement and deteriorate as [MATH]. The more robust Picard iteration converges only linearly. Rather than globalizing or preconditioning Newton's method, we modify the system to which it is applied. We the equation by introducing the flux [MATH] as an auxiliary (or ''lifting'') variable, apply a nonlinear to the resulting constitutive relation, , and the auxiliary variable by static condensation. Lifting alone leaves the linearization unchanged; it is the preceding transformation that yields the new method. The elimination is algebraic and pointwise at the quadrature points, so the flux variable is never discretized, no inf-sup condition or indefinite system arises, and the cost per iteration is that of a standard Newton step. Together with a pointwise feasibility bound on the lifting variable that keeps the diffusion tensor uniformly positive definite, this yields an iteration that we prove, in finite dimensions and for the [MATH]-Laplace equation, to converge globally and locally at a quadratic rate; a one-dimensional model problem explains why the lagged flux variable removes the zig-zag behavior of standard Newton for [MATH] close to one. Firedrake-based experiments for [MATH]-Laplace problems in two and three dimensions and for stationary and time-dependent [MATH]-Stokes flows show iteration counts largely insensitive to [MATH] and to mesh refinement, and up to an order of magnitude fewer iterations than standard Newton for [MATH] close to one.
tldr: The paper develops a robust Newton method for singular p-Laplace and p-Stokes equations by transforming the constitutive relation and lifting the flux as an auxiliary variable before linearization.
motivation: Newton's method for p-Laplace-type problems converges only near the solution, with iteration counts growing under mesh refinement and deteriorating as p approaches 1, while Picard iteration is more robust but only linearly convergent.
method: The equation is reformulated by introducing the flux as an auxiliary lifting variable, applying a nonlinear transformation to the constitutive relation, and eliminating the auxiliary variable via pointwise static condensation at quadrature points, avoiding inf-sup conditions or indefinite systems.
result: Global convergence and local quadratic convergence are proved in finite dimensions for p-Laplace, and Firedrake-based experiments in 2D/3D for p-Laplace and p-Stokes show iteration counts largely insensitive to p and mesh refinement, with up to an order of magnitude fewer iterations than standard Newton for p near 1.
conclusion: Transforming and lifting the constitutive relation before linearizing yields a provably robust and efficient solver for singular p-Laplace and p-Stokes problems, with cost per iteration comparable to a standard Newton step.

title: Error Bounds For The Sherman-Morrison Formula And Its Modification With Improved Stability
authors: Yuji Nakatsukasa Behnam Hashemi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is known that the Sherman--Morrison (SM) formula is not numerically stable. In recent work, we introduced SMIR, an algorithm that incorporates iterative refinement to enhance the SM backward error. In this paper we take a different route: adapting an algorithm of Govaerts, originally designed for general bordered linear systems, we develop a modified Sherman--Morrison (MSM) method whose built-in self-correction makes it surprisingly resilient. Whereas standard SM requires the solution of two [MATH] linear systems, MSM requires three; by contrast, SMIR requires [MATH] solves, where [MATH] is the number of IR steps and can be substantially larger than three, when IR converges slowly. We then derive backward and forward error bounds for both SM and MSM. The SM backward error bound established here is stronger than the one proved in [Hashemi \& Nakatsukasa 2026]: it accounts for every rounding error and holds with no conditions on the size of the capacitance. From these bounds we extract growth factors that are cheap to compute a posteriori and can be used to certify the backward and forward stability of SM and MSM on a given problem. In our experiments, MSM consistently produces backward stable solutions, and is therefore observed to be forward stable as well. A formal proof of the stability --- or instability --- of MSM remains an open problem.
tldr: The paper derives backward and forward error bounds for the Sherman-Morrison formula and proposes a modified Sherman-Morrison (MSM) method with improved numerical stability.
motivation: The standard Sherman-Morrison formula is known to be numerically unstable, and existing remedies such as the authors' earlier SMIR algorithm can require many iterative refinement solves, motivating a cheaper, self-correcting alternative.
method: Adapting Govaerts' algorithm for bordered linear systems, the authors construct MSM, which uses three linear solves instead of two, and derive rounding-error-aware backward and forward error bounds for both SM and MSM along with computable a posteriori growth factors.
result: The new SM backward error bound is stronger than the previous one and holds without conditions on the capacitance, while MSM is observed experimentally to be consistently backward stable (and hence forward stable), though a formal stability proof remains open.
conclusion: MSM offers a practical, resilience-improving alternative to standard Sherman-Morrison updates and to SMIR, with certifiable a posteriori stability bounds, but its theoretical stability characterization is left as an open problem.

title: The Ergodicity Of Geodesic Flows On Rank One Manifolds Of Nonpositive Curvature
authors: Xiaokai Liu Fei Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the ergodicity of the geodesic flows on closed rank one manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature. We introduce a subset of the manifold defined by the infinite-order vanishing of the Gaussian curvature in dimension two, or of the fiberwise second moment of the reduced Jacobi determinant in arbitrary dimensions, and derive bounds on the Liouville measure and Hausdorff dimension of the singular set in terms of this subset. In particular, if this subset has zero volume, then the singular set has zero Liouville measure, and the geodesic flow is ergodic with respect to Liouville measure. By extending this method to real analytic metrics, we characterize the singular set as the set of zeros of a nontrivial real analytic determinant constructed from curvature operators, thereby establishing ergodicity in this setting without any additional assumptions.
tldr: The paper studies ergodicity of geodesic flows on closed rank one manifolds of nonpositive curvature by bounding the singular set via a curvature-degeneracy subset and extending the argument to real analytic metrics.
motivation: Ergodicity of geodesic flows on rank one manifolds is a classical problem in Riemannian geometry and dynamical systems, and the authors aim to weaken or remove extra assumptions on the metric needed for such results.
method: They introduce a subset of the manifold defined by infinite-order vanishing of the Gaussian curvature (in 2D) or of the fiberwise second moment of the reduced Jacobi determinant (in general dimension), and bound the Liouville measure and Hausdorff dimension of the singular set in terms of it.
result: If that subset has zero volume, the singular set has zero Liouville measure and the geodesic flow is ergodic; for real analytic metrics the singular set is characterized as the zero set of a nontrivial real analytic determinant built from curvature operators, yielding ergodicity without additional assumptions.
conclusion: The work provides a general curvature-based criterion for ergodicity of geodesic flows, including an unconditional result for real analytic metrics on closed rank one manifolds of nonpositive curvature.

title: 3d Computational Modeling Of The Vascular Heat-Sink Effect In Microwave Ablation Of Tumors Close To The Aorta
authors: Youjin Kim, Kyungho Yoon, Minwoo Shin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microwave ablation (MWA) is a percutaneous ablation that induces thermal necrosis by generating localized high-temperature regions within tumor tissue. However, when a tumor is located close to a large vessel such as the aorta, blood flow continuously removes heat from the ablation zone. This phenomenon causes the vascular heat-sink effect and thereby increases the risk of incomplete ablation. This study constructs an ANSYS-based numerical framework to investigate the heat-sink effect during MWA of tumors located close to the aorta. The computational model consists of the tumor, surrounding tissue, vessel wall, blood flow domain, and microwave antenna. Microwave-induced heating was represented by an equivalent heat source mapped from the High-Frequency Structure Simulator (HFSS)-derived volume loss density, rather than by direct electromagnetic-thermal coupling within the thermal-fluid solver. Two parametric studies were performed to quantify the heat-sink effect. First, the tumor-aorta distance was varied at D = 0 mm, 4 mm, and 8.5 mm to assess how vessel proximity affects temperature elevation and ablation zone formation. Second, at each tumor-aorta distance, three blood-flow conditions were compared: no blood, stagnant blood V = 0 m/s, and normal aortic blood flow V=0.65 m/s. This comparison enabled the heat-sink effect of blood flow to be independently evaluated. The results highlight the clinical need for simulation-based treatment planning in patients with tumors located close to major vessels.
tldr: The paper builds an ANSYS-based computational model to study how aortic blood flow causes a vascular heat-sink effect during microwave ablation of nearby tumors.
motivation: Tumors adjacent to large vessels such as the aorta can experience incomplete microwave ablation because blood flow continuously removes heat from the ablation zone.
method: A 3D thermal-fluid model incorporating tumor, tissue, vessel wall, blood flow, and microwave antenna is used, with heating represented by an equivalent heat source mapped from HFSS-derived volumetric loss density; parametric studies vary tumor-aorta distance and blood-flow conditions.
result: Vessel proximity and blood flow reduce temperature elevation and ablation-zone formation, demonstrating the heat-sink effect for distances of 0, 4, and 8.5 mm and for no blood, stagnant blood, and normal aortic flow.
conclusion: The findings highlight the need for simulation-based treatment planning in patients with tumors near major vessels to avoid incomplete ablation.

title: A Strictly Convex And Smooth Banach Space With The Daugavet Property
authors: Sheldon Dantas, Jaan Kristjan Kaasik, Yo\"el Perreau
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct equivalent norms on [MATH], arbitrarily close to the usual [MATH]-norm, which are weakly midpoint locally uniformly rotund and G\^ateaux smooth, and whose dual norms have the Daugavet property. In particular, we obtain a strictly convex and smooth Banach space with the Daugavet property, thereby solving a longstanding open problem in the area.
tldr: The authors construct equivalent norms on a Banach space that are weakly midpoint locally uniformly rotund and Gâteaux smooth with duals having the Daugavet property, yielding a strictly convex and smooth Banach space with the Daugavet property.
motivation: The existence of a strictly convex and smooth Banach space with the Daugavet property was a longstanding open problem in Banach space geometry, requiring new renorming techniques.
method: The authors construct equivalent norms arbitrarily close to the usual norm on a given space using renorming techniques to simultaneously achieve weak midpoint local uniform rotundity, Gâteaux smoothness, and the Daugavet property in the dual.
result: They obtain equivalent norms with the desired geometric properties and thereby produce the first example of a strictly convex and smooth Banach space possessing the Daugavet property, resolving the open problem.
conclusion: The construction settles a long-standing question in nonlinear and isometric Banach space theory, demonstrating compatibility between strict convexity, smoothness, and the Daugavet property.

title: Second-Order Imex Time-Stepping Methods For Efficient Bidomain Multi-Electrode Array Simulations Of Cardiac Stem Cell Monolayers
authors: Sofia Tonali, Sofia Botti, Luca Franco Pavarino
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-electrode Arrays (MEAs) enable tissue-level electrophysiological studies of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) by recording extracellular field potentials. Recent computational models have improved MEA simulations by coupling detailed electrode descriptions with the Bidomain framework, a parabolic-elliptic system of nonlinear PDEs coupled with a stiff ionic model. The standard numerical strategy relies on operator splitting techniques that decouple the PDE and ODE components. In most implementations, the ionic subsystem is treated explicitly while the diffusive operator is handled implicitly, resulting in a first-order implicit-explicit (IMEX) time discretization. Although computationally convenient, this approach limits temporal accuracy and may reduce efficiency in large-scale simulations. In this work, we investigate higher-order IMEX Runge-Kutta schemes within a Strang-based operator splitting, specifically tailored for the MEA model of hiPSC-CMs monolayers. First- and second-order schemes are compared in terms of computational cost and global error against a high-fidelity reference solution obtained with a very small time step. For a fixed computational cost, the second-order schemes achieve errors that are 2-3 orders of magnitude smaller than those of the first-order method. These results demonstrate that higher-order IMEX integration significantly improves the accuracy-to-cost ratio of MEA simulations, providing a practical and reliable approach for large-scale electrophysiological studies.
tldr: This paper develops higher-order IMEX Runge-Kutta time-stepping schemes within Strang splitting for Bidomain multi-electrode array simulations of cardiac stem cell monolayers, achieving 2-3 orders of magnitude lower error than first-order methods at equal cost.
motivation: Standard MEA simulation implementations use first-order implicit-explicit discretizations of the parabolic-elliptic Bidomain system coupled to a stiff ionic model, which limits temporal accuracy and scaling efficiency for large-scale electrophysiological studies.
method: Second-order IMEX Runge-Kutta schemes are embedded in a Strang-based operator splitting framework for the Bidomain MEA model of hiPSC-CM monolayers, and compared against first-order schemes in terms of computational cost and global error relative to a high-fidelity reference solution.
result: For a fixed computational cost, the second-order schemes yield global errors 2-3 orders of magnitude smaller than the first-order method.
conclusion: Higher-order IMEX integration substantially improves the accuracy-to-cost ratio of MEA simulations, offering a practical and reliable numerical approach for large-scale cardiac electrophysiology modeling.

title: PIA-Bench: Towards Automated Privacy Impact Assessment With Large Language Models
authors: Jiamin Zheng, Hao-Ping Lee, Luo Mai, Jingjie Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.12571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy impact assessment (PIA) is a critical instrument for institutions to proactively identify privacy risks and develop mitigation strategies before system deployment. While mandated across regulatory and institutional contexts, executing PIA requires extensive privacy and technical expertise, posing a particular challenge for teams without access to such resources.
